idea.name: Post-final cash-out desk: rest a 99c bid on the winner after the game is decided
idea.family: sports / settlement mechanics (selling immediacy), incl. Kalshi's own live-score feed for other sports
idea.mechanism: Poll a free official feed: statsapi.mlb.com (ms-precision play times; Final ~30 s after the last play), ESPN's site.web.api.espn.com host (site.api.espn.com returns 403), api-web.nhle.com, or Kalshi's own GET /milestones + /live_data/{type}/milestone/{id} (status, winner, scores for tennis, table tennis, darts, cricket, esports). When the game shows Final/closed with a winner and no replay review is open, post a 99c bid on the winner (YES in the winner's market, NO in the loser's). Winners who want cash now sell into it; Kalshi closes ~4 min later (MLB median 256 s after the last out; NFL 45-127 s after ESPN's END GAME) and pays ~7 min after (MLB median 439 s). Earn 1c/contract minus a ~0.009-0.035c maker fee (MLB multiplier 0.5). Cancel on any correction. Can run on pinrun's idle cash between crypto entries, never blocking a hedge.
idea.why_mispriced: Nothing is mispriced: winners pay ~1c for immediacy (app sell button, reusing cash on the next game). Harmless flow; the only informed seller is one who knows the final play will be overturned.
idea.must_be_true: The queue already resting at 99c must be short enough that a bid posted ~30 s after the final fills before close. The evidence says probably NOT: in 39 of 40 MLB games post-final selling never pushed the price below 99c (resting bids exceeded the selling); decided markets showed 123k-179k contracts resting at 99c (ITF, Test cricket) and 66k-124k at 97-98c (WTA). If so, a late joiner gets almost nothing and the flow numbers are other people's queue position. Feed-final status must be reliable (walkovers, retirements, reviews, esports forfeits). Kalshi's own live feed is BEHIND the market by 8-13 s, so it must never be used as an in-play trigger.
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: $0-15/day, most likely $0-3; the queue decides. Ceiling ~$9/game at the full $900 bank filling every game, ~6-8 non-overlapping MLB cycles/day plus ~3 NFL Sunday windows (~$40/day if $900 turned over ~5 times fully filled). MLB regular season ends ~09-27.
idea.data_needed: One evening of 1/s read-only book polling from the last inning/last 2 minutes to close on ~10-20 MLB-postseason/NCAAF games: record 99c bid depth at the out and each second, post-final selling, and compute what a bid posted at +30 s would have filled. Kill if median fill < 100 contracts/game. For other sports: log feed-final time, Kalshi close time and 99c fills after feed-final on 50 matches.

chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
$900 bank: $0 a day as measured on tennis, table tennis, esports and darts (0 contracts filled after the finish; at 1c per contract that is $0). Best case, only if we somehow sat at the front of the queue: 900 x (1c - 0.009c fee) = about $8.92 per MLB game. The median MLB game sells 11,081 contracts after +30 s, so a front-row 900 would fill in about 3 games out of 4. The measured queue says we are never at the front: queues of 175k-450k per side on markets far smaller than MLB. Realistic: $0-1 a day.
$5k bank: also $0 as measured. Money is not the limit, the queue is. Front-row best case would be min(5,000, what the game sells) x about 1c, so under $50 a game, and still $0 behind the queue.
chk.worst_case: The play that ended the game gets overturned after we are filled: we lose 99c per contract, about -$891 at 900 contracts or -$4,950 at the $5k size. Bidding only after the official Final, with no review open, makes that very unlikely but not zero. Feed errors, retirements and esports forfeits are the remaining paths. 1) Queue position. The step is 1c and 99c is the top, so priority goes purely by time. On every finished market I watched, a queue of 170k-450k contracts per side, on both the winner-YES and loser-NO books, was already in place by the finish or appeared within about a minute. It is almost certainly an official-data-fed desk. Blowout college football games carry millions of contracts at 99c from before kickoff.
2) Almost no selling after the finish outside MLB and football: 0-266 contracts per side before Kalshi closed, 4-10 minutes later.
3) MLB's flow (median 11k after +30 s) is too small against any plausible queue, and the regular season ends 09-27.
4) An overturned final or a feed error costs 99c per contract, against 1c earned.
5) Sharing pinrun's cash risks blocking a hedge, and a gate must never block a hedge.

idea.name: In-play two-book parity and cross-series arithmetic breaks (buy both teams' YES under $1; quarter/half/team totals vs game)
idea.family: sports / in-play internal arbitrage
idea.mechanism: (1) Kalshi runs a SEPARATE book for each team (team A YES, team B YES); cancelled games settle at fair prices summing to ~$1. Stream both books; when ask_A + ask_B + both taker fees < $1, buy both at once fill-or-kill and hold for a sure $1. (2) Football arithmetic (whole-number scores, .5 strikes): 'part above x' implies 'game above x'; 'A above a' and 'B above b' imply 'game above ceil(a)+ceil(b)-0.5'; 'game above g' implies 'A above a' or 'B above b' when floor(a)+floor(b) < ceil(g); each gives a 2-3 leg package paying >= $1. Pregame these are all consistent, so only in-play breaks matter.
idea.why_mispriced: During fast in-play moves the market maker re-prices one book a moment before the other.
idea.must_be_true: Both asks exist at the same instant for longer than our round trip; trades within 1 s of each other do not prove this (one leg may have moved, or another bot may already sweep both). Legging leaves a directional position. Most of the measured pool is within 5 s of plays, stale-leg races we would likely lose.
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: $0-10/day (weak to moderate). Pool measured only for the last 15 min of 40 MLB games: $257 net at least 5 s away from any play, $768 within 5 s of plays.
idea.data_needed: A separate research websocket recorder of both team books (and football parts books) for one evening/one college-football Saturday; count seconds where asks sum to <= 0.98 and size at those moments.
idea.evidence_so_far: MLB tape, 40 games, last 15 min before the final out: 92 game-by-5-second episodes where both teams' YES were bought within 1 s at a combined <= 0.97 (min 0.80), 39 of them > 15 s from any play; after MLB fees 9,851 contracts / $257 away from plays, 16,188 / $768 near plays. The earlier tape found 92 sub-0.97 episodes in 40 games' last 15 minutes. If those states lasted 5 seconds, about 6.5 of the 510 closes should have caught one; 0 did (chance about 0.0015). The only money left is the race. The tape pool at full fee is $136 per 40 games' last 15 minutes, about $3.40 a game, or about $50/day across ~15 MLB games. That is the total for ALL participants. chk.worst_case:
Legging, the only way to run it, since Kalshi has no two-market order. One leg fills at a price that was about to go stale, and the other disappears. The bot is left holding one team through the play that caused the gap: a home run or touchdown moves the price 20-50c.

At 100 contracts on a 50c leg: $20-50 lost on one event, or about $10-15 to flatten at once (spread plus two taker fees of ~1.75c each). NFL regular-season ties exist (rare). The tie rule was not checked, but no package was positive anyway.

2) What the tape showed is stale-leg sniping lasting about 2 seconds or less (95% bound). Faster, co-located bots win that, and Kalshi's collateral netting on these events (MECNET) makes it free for them.

3) Adverse selection. The only time we would get both fills is when the stale leg has not been sniped, meaning the move was not real. When it was real, we get one leg filled and the other gone.

4) The MLB fee is ambiguous: series multiplier 0.5, but every event record says override 1. At 1x even the tape pool halves.

5) The football part books are thin (median NCAAF 2H market: 578 contracts lifetime) and the implications are loose, so fair package cost is well above $1.

idea.name: Sports combo desk: sell parlays to recreational requesters (markup, or Frechet-hedged near game end)
idea.family: combos/parlays (RFQ layer) x sports leg books
idea.mechanism: (a) Markup desk: answer combo RFQs on uncorrelated multi-game combos at the product of leg mids plus a markup, undercutting incumbents where their markup is fat (8+ legs), or take NO on combos priced above the product by more than fees. (b) Frechet form: for parlays with most legs finished or nearly decided (so the parlay is essentially its one live leg), quote only outside the bounds the leg books enforce -- sell parlay YES when its price exceeds the weakest leg and buy that leg (end-of-game books hold 100k+ at 99c); buy parlay YES below 1 - sum of leg loss prices and hedge with the losing side of each leg. Hedge within the confirmation window before confirming.
idea.why_mispriced: Parlay buyers are recreational and take the best quote; incumbents run a fixed markup and do not reprice against live leg books. Public reporting: takers lost $380M before fees since launch; makers earned $24M after fees in 4 weeks; average markup on uncorrelated non-NFL combos 3.1%; Moshrefi 2026 Table I: cross-game parlays at 1.005x the leg product at 5 legs, 1.066x at 8, 1.223x at 10.
idea.must_be_true: Same quoting-rights question as I06. Our leg fair values (Kalshi mids) are as good as incumbents' sportsbook-fed models. Capital: selling cheap parlays ties ~98c/contract to earn ~0.5c; on 20c combos the 3% markup (~0.6c) is eaten by the combo maker fee (~0.56c; 50% of taker; uncorrelated NFL exempt). Correlated legs make the markup fair. For (b): the markup still binds once most legs are decided, and legs are hedgeable within the window.

chk.measured:
Why it dies: once the combo maker fee is paid, undercutting the winning incumbent quote leaves about 1% of the premium. That is smaller than the error in our own fair price. At our capital it is worth at most ~$2.40/day at $900, and even that assumes everything goes our way.

1) LIVE CAPTURE WITH FRESH LEG PRICES. This fixes the late-mids flaw in the prior evidence. 1,330 executed combo trades between 12:32 and 12:43Z (8:32-8:43 AM ET, Friday). For each combo I read the leg order books a median of 3.0 s after the print (p90 4.8 s). File: check-I28/livepoll.jsonl, analysis in live_an.out.
Price paid vs product of leg mids, independent games, all legs <=10c wide, maker-sold side (the "markup"), then the same after the 0.035*P*(1-P) combo maker fee:
- 2 legs (n=115): 1.065x count-weighted, median 1.026. After fee: +3.9% of premium.
- 3-4 legs (n=141): 1.033x. After fee: +1.0%.
- 5-7 legs (n=146): 1.075x. After fee: +4.2%.
- 8-10 legs (n=152): 1.126x. After fee: +8.3%.
- 11+ legs (n=227): 1.235x. After fee: +15.9%.
Earlier '8+ legs +40.8%' mostly came from mids read minutes late.

2) IS THE MID PRODUCT BIASED LOW? When incumbents BUY combos (n=48), they pay 0.94-0.99x the mid product. So their two-sided quote straddles the mid product and the mid product is a fair center, not low.

3) UNDERCUT SIMULATION. Quote 0.1c under every executed price. Charge capital until the first losing leg or the last leg settles, using early close.
- Non-tennis tickets <=$90 risk: 136 trades, EV 1.14% of premium, 0.27% of capital per day.
- Non-tennis tickets <=$500 risk: 244 trades, EV 1.72% of premium, 0.21% per day.
- Including tennis, the <=$90 figure rises to 1.34% per day. The fat-markup tickets (>=5% over fair after fee) are dominated by live tennis: ITF 36% vs 3% of other tickets, Challenger 44% vs 14%. There the leg moves between the incumbent's quote and the print (15 s timer plus up to 30 s to confirm). That is pay for timer risk, not free edge.

4) WINNER'S-CURSE CHECK (drift.py, drift_b.json). I re-read 1,925 legs about 2-12 min after capture. Median drift of the fair was 0 in every markup class, and there was no drift toward the executed price. The window was too short to rule the curse out.

5) FRECHET FORM (b), frechet_detail.out. Out of 1,262 trades, one bound violation was positive after fees: +$40, a live ITF doubles leg that moved during the timer. The 13 lower-bound violations were all 0.2-1.3c inside the bound and -1.3 to -2.3c per contract after fees. The earlier 06Z sample found 0 of 37.

6) REALIZED OUTCOMES, yesterday 22:30-02:00Z (realized_an.out). 3,329 combo trades, of which 2,783 have every leg final. Maker-sold side: +$14.0k net on $84.4k premium, 90% interval [-$31.7k, +$52.5k]. It is dominated by single tickets (-$21.3k and +$11.7k) and is one night's correlated slate, so it tells us nothing about our edge.

7) FEES AND RULES. The API shows KXMVECROSSCATEGORY fee_type 'quadratic_with_combo_maker_fees' (series_fee.out). The 'half the taker rate' coefficient and the NFL-only exemption come from press (ingame.com). The primary fee PDF returned 429 twice, so this is not verified. If there were no maker fee, add about 2.8% of premium at P~0.2.
Rule 5.3 (CFTC filing): any Member may quote. The API create-quote docs name no eligibility gate. Oddpool counts 5 combo-only quoters answering in under 200 ms. Rule 5.3(g) forbids trading other markets on private RFQ information, which puts pre-hedging legs inside the confirm window at compliance risk.

Artefact check applied: mids are now fresh, same-game combos are excluded, wide-leg books are excluded, and in-play tennis is split out. After that, the edge that remains is inside mid-price noise: roughly ±1.7% for a 3-leg combo of 1c-wide ~50c legs.
chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
Upper bounds assume Kalshi leg mids are the true odds, we win every trade we undercut by 0.1c with no incumbent re-quote, and capital stays fully deployed. Supply is not the limit: about 11 combo trades per second. Capital is.

$900 bank, non-tennis tickets <=$90 risk: 0.27%/day x $900 = about $2.40/day at best. Realistic: about $0. The edge is 1.1% of premium and the fair-price error is about ±1.7%, and we would win exactly the trades where our fair is lowest. With in-play tennis included: 1.34%/day, about $12/day, but that markup coincides with legs moving during the RFQ timer, so it is risk pay.

$5k bank, tickets <=$500 risk: 0.21%/day x $5,000 = about $10/day at best. Realistic: about $0.

Frechet form (b): $0. One positive violation in 1,262 trades, explained by an in-play move.

It can never be verified. Daily swing at $900 deployed is about ±$114: ~40 tickets a day, average risk $35, average price about 0.21. Confirming $2.40/day at 2 sigma would take (2x114/2.4)^2, about 9,000 trading days.
chk.worst_case: Selling parlays means selling lottery tickets. At $900 fully deployed, about 26 open tickets averaging $35 risk (max $90 each). A chalk night where favorites win and a third of the sold parlays hit costs about -$250 to -$350. That is 100-150 days of the best-case EV. At $5k with $500 tickets, a chalk weekend costs about -$1.5k to -$2k. For scale, yesterday's market-wide sample had a single ticket that lost a maker $21.3k.
chk.killer_risks:
- Measured markup vs fresh mids after the combo maker fee is 1.0-4.2% of premium for 2-7 legs. That is inside fair-value noise.
- The large markups sit in 8+ leg combos priced 0.3-1.6c, which tie ~98c of capital to earn fractions of a cent (0.05-0.15%/day), or in in-play tennis, where they pay for timer risk.
- Winner's curse: we win only where our Kalshi-mid fair is below 5 incumbent bots that have sportsbook feeds and answer in under 200 ms, and they may re-quote.
- Lottery variance makes any real edge unprovable within months.
- Rule 5.3(g) makes hedging inside the confirm window a compliance risk. In-play combos may be high-volatility markets (2 s confirm, 3 s timer).
- The combo maker-fee coefficient is from press, not the fee PDF (429). If it were zero, EV would rise by about 2.8% of premium at P~0.2, which is the one thing that could revive the idea.
- The sample is 10 minutes on a Friday morning. Weekend-night NFL-only combos are exempt from the maker fee, but they are the cheap many-leg, capital-heavy kind.
chk.next_test:
Only worth running if the fee check revives it.
1) Cheapest decisive step: read the Kalshi fee schedule PDF for the exact combo maker coefficient and the NFL exemption. If the coefficient is 0.035, the idea stays dead.
2) If it is lower: build a read-only paper quoter from the RFQ WebSocket plus leg books. Price every RFQ, match it to its executed trade, and log the would-have-won set. For pre-game (not in-play) tickets <=$90 risk, compare our fair with an external no-vig sportsbook line (the-odds-api: $30/mo for 20k credits; free tier 500 credits).
Pass bar, over >=5 days including a college Saturday and an NFL Sunday, with >=300 would-have-won tickets:
- The external no-vig fair must sit at least 3% of premium below our quote minus fee on average.
- The leg-mid drift toward the executed price over the next 30 min must close less than 1/3 of the gap.
Only then run a 1-week live test quoting <=$10-risk RFQs, with operator sign-off, to measure how often we actually win against incumbents.
chk.capital_needed: None worth committing. It is capital-bound: each $1 of risk turns over about every 0.6-1 day and earns at best 0.2-0.3% per day on non-tennis tickets. A per-ticket cap of about 10% of the bank is needed because RFQ size is set by the requester (median premium $5.65; 90th percentile $47; 99th percentile $945).

idea.name: Pin supply through combo requests (requester side)
idea.family: combos x pin bot
markets: KXBTC15M and the other 15-min up/down series
idea.mechanism: The pin bot is limited by offers on the winning side (usable supply halved). In the last 45 s, CREATE an RFQ for a combo of 2-4 legs our model says are each 99.x% (e.g. BTC-no + ETH-no). A maker must quote the full size. Accept only if the quote is below our joint fair by more than the combo taker fee (0.07*p*(1-p): ~0.2c at 97c).
idea.why_mispriced: If combo makers price off the leg books, which lag the index in the last minute (the pin edge), their quote inherits the lag, at any size.
idea.must_be_true: Makers still quote crypto combos in the last 45 s (seen 7-44 s before close at 06:30Z). Their quotes are not wider than the stacked leg edges. Last look does not reject exactly the good ones. Coins move together, so a combo concentrates a correlated loss.
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: $0-10/day, unknown.
idea.data_needed: Sign-off to CREATE RFQs (no money moves unless we accept) on 20 closes, logging quotes against pinrun's fair. Read-only proxy meanwhile: combo trades in the last 45 s vs the product of pinrun fairs.
idea.evidence_so_far: At 06:30Z crypto combos traded at 7.1 s and 2.1 s before close (99.04c and 99.99c) with legs at 99.7-99.9%: makers are active that late. File: sweep/sports-props-parlays-futures/closecombo_0630.out.

chk.measured:
THE IDEA'S MECHANISM IS REFUTED. Combo makers do not copy the lagging leg prices. They price near-certain combos close to 100c. What is left is a thin edge that depends on the tail, and its sign is not proven.

Data (all read-only; about 450 signed GETs plus the index tape on disk):
- 38 closes sampled, one every 75 minutes from 09-23 17:45Z to 09-25 12:15Z.
- For each close I listed every combo that closes then with GET /markets?series_ticker=KXMVECROSSCATEGORY&min/max_close_ts. That came to 63,650 combos, 31,204 of them made only of crypto 15-min legs.
- I pulled every trade from 62 s before the close to 2 s after (largest window 18,042 trades, so none was cut off at the 20,000 cap).
- Each leg was priced from the CF index at the trade second: the prints already locked in plus a random-walk remainder, with sigma from the last 300 s.
- Self-check: my index-derived outcomes AND-ed across legs matched Kalshi's recorded combo result on 22,349 of 22,349 combos. Strikes and settlement are therefore right.
- 16 of the 38 closes had no priced trades. Nine index hours are missing from disk, all between 09-23 16Z and 09-24 00Z.

Findings:
1. Makers price the index, not the stale leg books. Accepted combo asks when every leg was at z>=3 ran 97.0 to 99.99c, median about 99.5c. When every leg was at z>=5 and 20 s or less remained, asks were 99.47 to 99.99c. Asks of 96 to 99c appear only when a leg is genuinely at risk (z 2.4 to 4). The pin buys the same kind of legs at up to 98c.
2. Requesters who bought near-certain combos (model joint fair >= 0.97) in the last 45 s: 75 trades, 22 closes, 6,836 contracts. The same trades priced three ways:
   - pin-style model: +$29.90 (+0.44c a contract);
   - model with sigma x1.5: -$110.34;
   - index-measured flip rates: +$14.23 (+0.21c a contract). These rates come from results/MODEL_CALIBRATION_2026-09-25.md section 2, which covers 2,140 closes. For legs above 0.999 a leg lost 0.156% of the time at 45 s, 0.052% at 30 s, 0.039% at 20 s, 0.027% at 15 s, and 0 in about 19,000 cells at 10 s and at 5 s. I used 3/19,000 as the upper bound there.
   - By time left, index-measured: 45 s -0.27 to -0.58c; 30 s +0.1 to +0.2c; 20 s +0.13c; 15 s +0.37 to +1.05c; 10 s +0.18 to +0.25c. 47 of the 75 trades were positive.
   - $7.95 of the $14.23 is ONE trade: 4,612 contracts at 99.66c, 10 s before the 09-24 11:15Z close. The other 21 closes made +$6.28 on 2,224 contracts, about 0.28c a contract.
3. Settlement: 0 combo failures in 209 near-certain combo trades in the last 45 s, across 25 closes. That only bounds the failure rate below about 1.4% per trade. Break-even is about 0.2 to 0.3%, so the sample has no power to settle the question.
4. Size is not the limit. Accepted sizes ran from 0.1 to 4,612 contracts. Separately, 21 of 402 combos first requested in the last 45 s ever traded (5%). That count mixes 'no quote came' with 'requester declined', so it is not a quote rate.
5. RFQ rules, from docs.kalshi.com/getting_started/rfqs: all combo markets are 'high volatility'. The maker has 3 s to confirm after we accept, then a 1 s timer before execution. That is a 3 to 4 s last look. Series fee_type is quadratic_with_combo_maker_fees with multiplier 1, so the requester pays about 0.07*p*(1-p): about 0.03c at 99.6c.
6. Side lead, not I29: the MAKER side of combo cash-outs, where the requester SOLD a near-certain combo in the last 45 s. 134 trades, 22 closes, 10,365 contracts, +$122.52 index-measured (+1.18c a contract) for the makers who bought, 0 failures. Two caveats: those prices already won against other makers, and I did not check whether a retail API account may answer RFQs as a quoter.

chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
These numbers use the index-measured edge of about 0.2c a contract. That edge was seen only on OTHER requesters' accepted quotes, which are the quotes they chose to take. We have never seen a quote to us.

$900 bank:
- A single failure must stay inside the $200 daily loss cap, and it lands on top of the pin's loss in the same coin. So size has to stay near 100 contracts a combo.
- 100 x 0.2c = $0.20 a close. Near-certain late combo buys happened on 22 of 38 sampled closes, about 55 closes a day, giving about $11 a day at best.
- One failure costs about $100, which is roughly 9 days of that.
- With sigma x1.5 the same trades are negative (-$110 on 6,836 contracts).
- Realistic: $0 to 10 a day, sign unproven.

$5k bank:
- About 500 contracts a close x 0.2c = $1 a close, about $55 a day at best.
- One failure is about -$500.
- Realistic: $0 to 50 a day, sign unproven.

The capital constraint is small: combos settle about 6 minutes after the close (settlement_ts 06:35:58Z for the 06:30Z close), so the money is back before the next quarter hour. The binding constraint is tail risk against a 0.2c margin.
chk.worst_case:
One leg flips in the last 10 to 15 s. The combo pays $0, so the whole stake is lost: about $100 at the $900-bank size, about $500 at $5k. The legs are the same coins at the same close the pin trades, so the same move also takes the pin's position in that coin (about $88 at size 88).
- Combined at $900: about -$190 to -$300 in one close, which is 20 to 33% of the bank and hits the $200 day cap.
- A fast crash that flips several coins at once costs the combo nothing extra, since it can only go to $0 once, but it costs the pin once for each coin.
chk.killer_risks:
1. The margin is thinner than our knowledge of the tail. Break-even is about 0.2 to 0.3% combo failure. The index-only table covers 22 days, 2,140 closes. A once-a-month flash move would flip the sign. Makers quoting 99.6c are pricing a fatter tail than our table, and they may be right.
2. The last look lets makers pick against us. They get 3 s to confirm after we accept, plus a 1 s timer. They confirm when a leg has just become riskier, which makes their sale better, and can decline when it became safer. The index table cannot see this. Rule 5 applies: a tape loss rate is not our loss rate. The pin's live loss rate is about 40 times the tape's for the same reason.
3. We have no quote to us, only accepted quotes to others. Those are the best a requester chose to take. Only 5% of combos first requested in the last 45 s ever traded.
4. Half of the measured edge is one 4,612-contract trade.
5. The exposure is correlated with the pin's own legs, so it doubles up on the one event we already lose on.
6. The fair here is my own simplified model, not pinrun.fair. It is exact on outcomes (22,349 of 22,349), but z-band placement near 0.999 could differ from pinrun's. Legs at z>=5 are not affected.
7. Repeatedly creating RFQs without accepting may breach Kalshi RFQ etiquette or terms. Unchecked.
chk.next_test:
Step 1, costs nothing: RFQ-only watcher. It creates an RFQ each close and never accepts, so no money moves. It still needs operator OK, because it sends non-GET calls and the sweep is read-only.
- On at least 100 closes, about 18 s before the close, request a combo of 2 to 4 coins whose pinrun.fair is >= 0.999, at 100 contracts.
- Log every quote: price, size, the second it arrives, the pinrun fair at that second, and the index-measured flip rate for that time left.
- Pass bar, all three:
  - a quote at or below 99.75c arrives by 8 s before the close on at least 70% of closes;
  - the median best ask is at or below 99.70c;
  - the edge after fee, using the index-measured flip rate, is >= +0.15c a contract.
- Fail if the median ask is >= 99.85c. At that price the edge is under 0.1c and the idea is dead.

Step 2, only if step 1 passes: live combos at 5 to 10 contracts, one per close, with per-order sign-off. Log every maker confirmation and decline. Proving our failure rate is under 0.25% takes about 1,200 combos with 0 failures, about 13 days at 96 closes a day. That is the true decisive cost.

Side lead worth its own check, answering cash-out RFQs as a maker (+1.18c a contract on 10,365 contracts): first confirm with Kalshi that a retail API account may quote RFQs. Then measure how far above the winning bids we would have to bid to win.
chk.capital_needed: About $100 of the $900 bank per close. It is back within about 6 minutes of each close, but it sits at the same close as the pin's stake. At $5k, about $500 a close.

ref.strongest_objection:
I could not refute the checker's verdict; I could only make it narrower. On the index tape the sign comes out positive, better than the checker found. Three concrete problems cut the dollars and change how it must be tested:

(1) The good prices were not from one ask. The accepted prices came from bots already running this exact trade, and each asked about 10 times per fill.
- On the 45 combos where someone bought a near-certain combo late: 5,227 quote requests (RFQs) in the last 60 s against 85 buy fills.
- Same-size requests before each fill: median 10.5.
- Bot-sized buyers (4,612, 478, 391, 263 and 119 contracts) took 11 to 15 requests each, one every 1 to 2 s, starting 25 to 33 s before the close.
- So the checker's step 1 (a single request at 18 s before the close, passing if 70% of closes get a quote at or below 99.75c) will mostly come back empty. That is a false 'dead'. A working version has to re-ask every second, and it competes with bots that already do.

(2) The cheapest-looking quotes are the dangerous ones. This was measured on actual combo fills in the checker's 38-close sample.
- Requester buys priced more than 3c below the model's fair: 30 trades in 7 closes. The model expected 5.4 failures; there were 9, and they lost $916 on 1,791 contracts.
- Buys 0 to 3c below fair: 1.6 failures expected, 2 actual, +$54.
- At 09-24 20:00Z makers sold combos at 30 to 37c that the model priced at 71 to 74c, 58 to 60 s before the close. XRP jumped between 60 and 55 s before the close and DOGE crossed its strike about 50 s before. The makers priced the jumps up to 5 s before the index-based model saw them, and every one of those buys lost.
- The idea's rule ('accept if below our fair') picks exactly these quotes. How strong this effect is on near-certain combos is unmeasured: 0 failures in 53 fills.

(3) Every combo number comes from a quiet 9-day window.
- All-crypto combos first appear 09-17: 0 listed at 09-10, 09-13, 09-15 and 09-16 12:00Z; 92 at 09-17.
- The tape's two crash-type late flips both came before that:
  - 09-11 12:30Z: a 0.5% crypto-wide jump starting 33 s before the close flipped 6 of 9 legs that sat at z 4 to 13.5 thirty seconds out. Every one of them was 99.99% or better on the model.
  - 09-12 03:00Z: BTC jumped $66 ten seconds before the close and flipped a leg at z = 11, 15 s out.
- The checker's '0 failures in 209' has never seen one. Also, 0 combos were listed for 07:30, 08:45 and 09:00Z on 09-24, so the product can go dark.

Correlation: an event like 09-11 costs the combo its whole stake, about $100 at 100 contracts, plus the pin's stake in up to 6 coins in the same close.

Ceiling about $14 a day: 100 contracts x about 0.3c (tape edge at the upper failure bound) x half of 96 closes, and only by re-asking every second the way the competing bots do. One failure is about -$100, roughly 7 to 12 days of profit, and it lands in the same close as a pin loss. At $5k: $0 to 40 a day. The test also needs two changes: re-ask every second instead of once, and cap how far below our fair we will accept (for example, ignore quotes more than about 1c under fair), because the deepest discounts are the ones that lost.

idea.name: Pre-game MLB prop maker with a lineup guard
idea.family: player props (making)
idea.mechanism: MLB HR props sit with 10-14c spreads (e.g. 1c/15c, 6c/17c). Rest bids and offers inside the spread pre-game only; cancel instantly when the MLB Stats API posts the lineup or a scratch; cancel all at first pitch.
idea.why_mispriced: Retail prop and parlay buyers cross wide spreads; the incumbent quotes wide to cover in-game pickoff risk, which a pre-game-only maker avoids.
idea.must_be_true: Enough pre-game volume crosses (unmeasured). Pre-game information events (lineups, weather, scratches) are caught by the guard. Makers pay no fee (quadratic x0.5, no maker fee).
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: $0-20/day, unknown; MLB in season only ~6 months (regular season ends ~09-27).
idea.data_needed: One day of HR-prop trade tape split pre-game vs in-game with the quoted spread at each pre-game trade, plus statsapi lineup-post times.
idea.evidence_so_far: Snapshot: 83 open HR markets with typical 10-14c spreads (sweep/sports-props-parlays-futures/props_snapshot.json). Pre-game prices are well calibrated (see I60), so the edge would come from the spread, not direction.

chk.measured:
Source: the Kalshi trade tape, 1-minute book candles and settlements, plus MLB Stats API first-pitch times. This is tape, not our fills, so it cannot tell us our own loss rate. Sample: 13 MLB games on 2026-09-23 and 09-24, 317 prop markets (all HR 1+ markets in those games, plus samples of HR 2+, HIT, TB and HRR), 11,050 pre-game trades, about 1.75M pre-game contracts. Clustered by game.

1) The idea's premise is wrong. The 10-14c spreads are on markets where almost nothing trades. Contract-weighted, 76% of pre-game volume traded when the spread was 1c, 22% at 2-3c, 2.2% at 4c or more, and 0.1% at 10c or more.

2) Flow: 67% of HR volume is pre-game, about 133k contracts per game at an average price of 13.5c. 94% of it is takers buying YES, so a maker ends up short YES.

3) What the resting side earned on pre-game flow, measured against the mid at first pitch: +1.0c per contract (SE 0.24). On markets whose book was tight at first pitch (2c or less, the cleanest fair value) it was only +0.25c per contract. So the 1c-spread flow, which we can only join from the back of the queue, is worth about 0.25-0.8c.

4) The only piece a newcomer can improve on is flow that traded while the spread was 4c or wider: 2,852 contracts per game. Quoting 1c better than the resting ask gives +1.59c per contract against the first-pitch mid, or about +0.93c on the tight-closing-book subsample. If we took only the first 10 or 50 contracts of each such trade, that is 215 or 787 contracts per game, worth $3.63 or $14.65 per game, assuming we win every one of them (100% capture). Measured against settlement the same flow is +7.4c ± 4.2c. Overall settlement P&L is +0.7c ± 3.2c, so the settlement check can only detect effects of about ±6c and cannot confirm or refute the edge.

5) Wide spreads are usually brief: median 2 minutes, 90th percentile 109 minutes. 21% of wide-spread volume trades within 5 minutes of a market listing.

6) Kalshi lists most players' markets only after lineups post (about 1.5-2.3 hours before first pitch). Only star players' markets open the night before. So the lineup guard barely matters: star-market flow before the lineup earned +0.51c (SE 0.42), after it +0.78c.

7) A scratched player settles at a 'fair market price', not NO. About 5% of HR markets settled this way, at about the pre-game price (e.g. Stowers settled at 0.11 against a last trade of 0.11). The idea's stated worst case of -15c per contract is wrong; a scratch costs about 1-2c.

8) Fees, read from /series: fee_type 'quadratic', multiplier 0.5, so makers pay no fee. No liquidity-incentive program covers MLB props.

9) Extension check on NFL anytime-TD props (KXNFLTD), 3 games, 18.3M pre-game contracts: dead for this approach. 96% of volume trades at a 1c spread, the book at kickoff is 1c wide, the resting side earns +0.22c per contract, and wide-spread flow is 237 contracts per game.

chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
None of this is measured on our own fills. It rests on the tape plus an assumed share of fills we would win.

Common inputs:
- Edge per contract: +0.93c (robust) to +1.6c, measured against the first-pitch mid.
- Available flow on a full slate of about 14 games, taking at most 50 contracts from each trade: about 11k contracts per day.
- Cash tied up: about 85c per short-YES contract, held from the fill (0-2 hours pre-game) until the game ends about 3 hours after first pitch. That allows about 1.5 cycles per day.

$900 bank: capital binds at about 1,000 contracts open at once, so about 1,500 contracts per day. 1,500 × 0.93-1.6c = $14-24 per day, and only if we win at least 14% of the eligible flow with no worse picks than the tape shows. A realistic range is $0-15 per day.

$5k bank: capacity is about 8k contracts per day, so the limit becomes how much flow we win. At 25-50% of 11k that is 2.7-5.5k contracts × 0.93-1.6c = $25-90 per day at best; realistically $10-50.

Timing: this only works in-season. The MLB regular season ends 09-27, which leaves 2 days. The postseason has 1-4 games per day in October, then nothing until late March 2027. NFL gives $0, per item 9 of the measurements.
chk.worst_case:
The position is short HR YES at about 15c, which loses about 85c per contract when the player homers.

At the $900 size, about 1,000 contracts spread over about 60 players (about 17 each): a day with 3 standard deviations of extra homers (16 homers against 7.8 expected) loses about $119, and an extreme slugfest slate about $150-200. That is roughly 15-20% of the bank, or 8-15 days of expected profit.

Single-player risk: 50 contracts on one player who homers costs about $42.

A scratch is small (about 1-2c per contract) because scratched players settle at a fair price.

At $5k with about 5k contracts, scale these by about 5x: a -$600 day.
chk.killer_risks:
(1) Capture is unmeasured. The +1.6c assumes our improved quote is at the best price, alone, whenever a taker crosses. A pro market maker that tops our price or tightens within seconds cuts that share toward zero. The tape cannot show how they react.

(2) Our fills could be worse than the tape's. Improving a wide book invites takers who would not have crossed the old ask, including sharp prop bettors pricing off sportsbook lines. The per-contract edge on the flow we actually get could turn negative. This is the same lesson as MAKER_SIM on the 15-minute crypto markets and the live-versus-tape 31x gap.

(3) The edge depends on the fair-value yardstick. Against the first-pitch mid it fell from +1.0c to +0.25c when restricted to books that were tight at first pitch. Settlement cannot confirm it: the check only detects effects of about ±6c.

(4) The main flow (76% at a 1c spread) cannot be improved on. Joining the queue there is worth 0.25-0.8c, from behind the incumbent.

(5) Seasonality: 2 regular-season days remain, then a thin postseason, then 6 months with nothing. NFL, the in-season substitute, is measured dead.

(6) Variance: short-lottery payoff, daily standard deviation about $50 against about $10 expected at $900. It would take about 100 in-season days to confirm a real edge at 2 standard errors.

(7) Build cost: a live quoting engine for about 300 markets per day, with cancel-at-first-pitch logic. It shares a rate limit with the live bot.
chk.next_test:
Cheapest decisive test, zero risk: a postseason paper watcher. Record the WebSocket book and trades for every HR 1+ market from listing to first pitch. Simulate one rule: 'when the YES spread is 4c or wider with bid above 0, offer YES at ask - 1c, at most 10 contracts per market, cancel at first pitch'. Count a fill only when a taker-YES trade at or above our price arrives at least 1 second after our simulated post. Because our quote would be alone at a new best price, this paper fill is an honest upper bound. What it cannot show is how the incumbent reacts.

Pass bar for the paper watcher, written before any number is seen: at least 20 games and at least 150 simulated fills, mean markout against the first-pitch mid of at least +0.8c per contract, on markets whose book at first pitch was 2c or tighter.

If that passes, and with per-order operator sign-off: a live test at 5 contracts per market in the same postseason, 1-contract clips where possible. Pass bar: at least 100 live fills with markout against the first-pitch mid of at least +0.5c per contract, and a live fill rate of at least 25% of the paper watcher's fill count. Anything less means the incumbent is taking the flow or we are being picked off, and the idea is dead.

If the postseason gives too few games, park it until MLB Opening Day 2027. Do not build for NFL.
chk.capital_needed: $900 is enough for the test and for a capital-bound version: about 1,000 contracts open at once, about $850 tied up. $3-5k lets it use the flow, if capture holds.

ref.strongest_objection:
The checker's money figure assumes the ~$900 bank is free to hold MLB positions, and it is not. The live crypto bot sizes from Kalshi's gross cash balance (`read_bank()` reads `/portfolio/balance`, pinrun.py:15045). Cash falls when a position is opened, and the bot shrinks its bets immediately when cash falls ("DOWN IS IMMEDIATE"). It halts when cash is 20% below its high-water mark (`MAX_DRAWDOWN = 0.20`), and that halt holds until the operator re-bases it. Resting orders also reserve cash that the balance never shows (results/THE_PLAN.md: "Do resting orders reserve cash? Yes, cumulatively. balance_dollars is GROSS and never shows it"), so a book of prop quotes could make the bot's own orders, including hedges, fail on funds.

So a same-account prop maker has to stay under about $210 of tied-up cash, or the live bot halts (20% of about $1,043). At that size (about 235 open short-YES contracts, about 350 fills a day) and a robust edge of 0.3-1.1c per contract, it grosses about $1.0-3.9 a day, assuming we win every fill. The live bot loses about $1.2 a day of profit from the smaller bets during the ~6 hours the cash is tied up: about $26 a day lifetime × 19% × 6/24.

Net: about -$0.2 to +$2.7 a day at 100% capture, before any incumbent reaction or adverse selection from our own quotes. It gets worse:
- **The checker's own paper-test rule** (at most 10 contracts per market) gives only 65 contracts and $0.60 per game, again assuming we win every fill, on my independent days.
- **The robust edge did not hold up.** On markets whose book was 2c or tighter at first pitch, the checker's +0.93c came out +0.28c ± 0.25c on my days.
- **The calendar:** 45 regular-season games over 09-25..27, then at most 53 postseason games at 1-4 a day, the last on 10-31, then nothing until spring 2027.

idea.name: Mention-market ASR sniper (buy YES the moment a listed word is said)
idea.family: mentions: live speech-to-text on the broadcast
idea.mechanism: Stream the event's live audio (White House / C-SPAN, earnings webcast) into a streaming ASR engine (~0.3 s delay; ~$0.46 per audio hour with Deepgram). Match the transcript to the event's word list using Kalshi's rules (exact word or plural/possessive only). On a confident match buy YES up to 90-95c from whatever sells before the book reprices; hold to settlement.
idea.why_mispriced: Other side: stale YES sellers (NO bidders) who have not heard the word yet, and humans on delayed streams. Measured repricing is slow: median 68 s from the first print >= 60c to the first >= 95c.
idea.must_be_true: Our audio-to-order delay beats the humans and bots already racing: some words reprice in 0-4 s (TARI 3.2 s, BIDE 3.5 s, RADI 1.6 s), so the slow median may partly be ambiguous utterances. The source stream's own latency (web streams can lag 5-20 s behind broadcast) is not measured. ASR catches the right forms; Kalshi staff resolve by video, so a mishear is a full loss.
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: $5-30/day, uncertain: ~4 Trump events/week x ~6 YES words, if 100-300 contracts per word at ~15-20c edge.
idea.data_needed: Record 2-3 live Trump events: ASR word timestamps next to the Kalshi trade tape polled read-only every 1 s; measure our lead in seconds and contracts available at <= 95c after our timestamp.
idea.evidence_so_far: KXTRUMPMENTION trades, 8 settled events, 51 YES words with a detectable jump: in [jump-60 s, jump+30 s] takers bought 45,428 YES contracts below 95c (8,619 < 60c, 10,219 at 60-80c, 26,590 at 80-95c); 60c->95c median 68 s, p90 275 s. Kalshi closes all of an event's markets together at event end (no post-event window). Files: sweep/entertainment-mentions-companies/jump_race.py, KXTRUMPMENTION_settled.jsonl.gz.

chk.measured:
Source: Kalshi trade tape only (read-only, about 180 signed GETs). It measures supply and speed. It says nothing about how often WE would lose. Events: 8 KXTRUMPMENTION events (the earlier agent's file), plus KXTRUMPMENTIONB-26SEP24, KXFEDMENTION-26SEP and KXEARNINGSMENTIONCOST-26SEP24. That covers 11 events from 2026-09-11 to 09-24 and 395 markets. Costco is not settled yet, so its outcomes come from the last price. Files are in C:/Users/Joe/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--kals-repo/47b37ac1-655c-4d72-a81b-a48e9625d5bd/scratchpad/sweep/check-I31/ (race3.py/.out, final.py, final80.out, final60.out, split.py, paths.py, slow.py, tmb.jsonl.gz, cost_prov.jsonl.gz).

(1) The premise is false. When a listed word is said, one buyer's single order takes the whole cheap book at one timestamp. For 81 YES words, the time from the decisive move to the first print at 95c or higher: median 0.5 s, p25 0.0 s. Sample paths: BALL 0.21 to 0.84 at +0.0 s and to 0.99 at +0.4 s. Fed INDE 0.26 to 0.99 in one order, 1,282 contracts at 0.98. The idea's '68 s median' is a measurement artefact. It counted from the first print of 60c or more in the prior 300 s, which catches price drift as the topic comes up. I checked FEMA, SAUD and COMM by hand. Each drifted first, then was swept to 95c or more in under 1 s when the word was actually said (COMM's move came about 36 min before the speech).

(2) What a slower bot could get. Clean utterances (52 YES words, 9 events, 95c reached within 2 s): the first buyer's order took 29,784 contracts. Contracts traded at 95c or less more than 5 s later: 1,196, worth at most $77 across all 9 events. That is about $5.50/day as a ceiling. It assumes we beat every later buyer and never buy a word that settles NO.

(3) False alarms are large and common. Of 40 sharp jumps (from under 60c to 80c or more within 15 s, whatever the outcome), 12 settled NO. The first buyers made +$3,323 net over those 10 events, after losing $3,144 on NO words. Examples: KXTRUMPMENTION-26SEP24-BIDE, 7,190 contracts bought up to 0.91, lost $885. KXFEDMENTION-26SEP-QE, 842 contracts up to 0.99, lost $773. FRAU lost $592 and GOODS $410.

(4) A bot that follows the jump (ceiling, including words the crowd wrongly bought), over 10 events in 14 days: 0.5 s late at 90c or less: -$210. 1 s: -$363. 2 s: -$586. 5 s: -$708. At a 95c limit: +$12, -$199, -$498, -$651. Negative at every delay of 1 s or more.

(5) Slow words, where the crowd took 2-600 s to reach 95c: +$345 ceiling on YES words only over about 14 days, leaving out COMM. That is at most about $25/day before false alarms. It comes from about 7 words, and on exactly those words the crowd doubted whether the word counted.

(6) The Costco earnings call shows the same pattern: median 0.0 s to 95c, 2 NO-settled jumps, and $76 ceiling for a bot 2 s late.

Not measured: our own audio-to-order delay, and how far behind the room the public streams are.
chk.realistic_dollars_per_day: $900 bank: about $0/day, and more likely negative. With a public web stream plus ASR we would realistically be 2-5 s or more behind the first buyer. The ceiling after clean utterances is $77 over 14 days, about $5.50/day, and that assumes no false alarms and beating every other late buyer. Following jumps as they happen, including the crowd's false alarms, is -$586 to -$708 over 14 days, about -$42 to -$50/day. Words where the crowd hesitated add at most about $345/14 days, about $25/day, before our own false alarms. At a 90c entry the win is about 10c minus about 1c fee, and a wrong call loses about 90c. So we must be right about 91 times out of 100, and nothing shows we can be on the doubted words. One mistake at 300 contracts (-$255) wipes out any of these ceilings for weeks. $5k bank: the same. The limit is contracts for sale, not money. The only pot of money that exists is the first buyers' share: +$3,323 net over 14 days, about $237/day, split among everyone racing, and it cost them $3,144 in false alarms. Our share of that is unmeasured and on a home laptop is probably about 0.
chk.worst_case: One wrong match (a reporter says the word, a quoted clip, a form that doesn't count), bought at 0.80-0.95 at the proposed 100-300 contracts: -$80 to -$285 per mistake. Several words from the same event can be wrong at once, because they share one speaker, one audio stream and one ASR error mode. The fastest buyers' own measured mistakes: -$885 (7,190 contracts, Trump 09-24 BIDE) and -$773 (Fed QE bought at 0.99).
chk.killer_risks: 1. The whole supply of cheap contracts goes in one sub-second order from established buyers. A follower gets about 5% of the clean-utterance supply, worth $77 across 9 events. 2. Those fast buyers settle NO on 12 of 40 sharp jumps. Buying before the sentence is fully heard means buying false alarms, and waiting to be sure means buying nothing. 3. Public web streams run about 5-20 s behind the room (not measured here). The incumbents react within about 0.5 s of each other, so they almost certainly have a faster audio source. 4. Rules traps: only the named speaker counts, only exact or plural/possessive forms count, and Kalshi staff decide by video. The crowd's worst losses look like exactly these (BIDE, QE, FRAU, 26SEP21-BALL). 5. All of an event's markets close together at the end of the event, so there is no time after the event to trade. 6. Polymarket US offers no mention markets, so there is no cross-venue angle.
chk.next_test: Only one path is left: beat the incumbents to the audio. Test it read-only and free before writing any trading code. On 2-3 live Trump or White House events, run streaming ASR on the fastest source we can get. Try the White House YouTube live stream in low-latency mode and C-SPAN, and log each source's delay. At the same time, subscribe read-only to Kalshi's WebSocket trade channel for that event's tickers. For every listed word, record three times: our ASR first-hit time, the first-sweep time on the tape, and the settled result. Pass bar, written before looking: on at least 20 clean utterances, our first hit is at least 0.5 s BEFORE the first sweep on 50% or more of them, AND our hits are right on 95% or more of words after settlement (including speaker and word-form rules). If our hit comes after the sweep on most words (the expected result), the idea is closed for good. Cost: about $0.50 per audio hour of ASR, plus a few hours of recording.
chk.capital_needed: Small but lumpy. The incumbents' single orders ran $100 to $6,500 (up to 7,190 contracts). At our size, 100-300 contracts at about 0.9 is $90-270 per word. Money is tied up from the utterance until the event ends and Kalshi staff settle it (minutes to hours). Capital is not the limit; speed and precision are.

Only 12,237 traded 10 s or more after the first 5c move, and 11,780 at 30 s or more. In 44% of jumps the last cheap trade came within 1 s of the move; the median was 19 s.

2) Real value, measured against the price after the jump (not the settlement), after taker fee: $7,064 in total, $2,655 for trades 10 s or later, $2,539 for trades 30 s or later. That is money shared by EVERYONE who arrived late, over 47 days. The clean case is the only one a page scraper can be sure of: 'the score crossed the line', where the price ends at or below 15c or at or above 85c. There were 14 such jumps in 10 movies. After 10 s only 966 contracts were left, worth $205 in total, about $4.40 a day for all late arrivers combined. The rest are part-way jumps that ended between 15c and 85c: $2,450 after 10 s. 75% of that came from three movies (ONS, SUPER, ONE), and 24 of those 70 jumps went the wrong way at settlement.

3) The fastest traders were often wrong, which is the opposite of 'farmer quotes are stale'. There were 12 one-second sweeps: 7 right and 5 wrong at settlement. The two biggest were both wrong: ONS-66 (3c to 35c, 4,878 contracts) and INS-60 (11c to 36c, 4,793 contracts). In the largest cases the resting quotes were correct and the sweeper lost. Someone reading an exact RT count should almost never be wrong, so this also counts against 'the trigger is the RT count'.

4) Does the price hold? Across all 84 jumps, the direction held at settlement 59 times and failed 25 times. Measured against the price 1 h later, value for trades 30 s or later falls from $2,539 to $1,902.

5) The RT page: the plain URL is behind Akamai with cache-control max-age of 88 to 120 s, so a simple poller can be up to 2 minutes late. A cache-busted URL (?cb=random) returned a fresh page with a different ETag, so a fast read is possible for anyone, including rivals. The review list API returned 401 (login needed) and the reviews page loads in the browser, so there are no past review timestamps. Whether RT or the critics' own sites move first CANNOT be measured from history.

6) SPIN-OFF, a separate idea from the tape only, so it is a hypothesis and not evidence: 'follow the jump'. Buy the jump's direction at the last traded price 1 h after the jump and hold to settlement. 82 jumps, 18 movies, 57 of 82 won, average entry 58c. Averaged per movie: +12.3c a contract (t 3.19) at last-trade price, +9.7c (t 2.40) with 3c extra cost, +7.4c (t 1.73) with 6c. Both halves of the sample were positive: +8.0c and +11.5c at +3c cost. Leaving out any one movie gives t between 2.06 and 3.45. Live spreads at active KXRT strikes run 2 to 13c, so the 6c row is the realistic one, and it is NOT significant. Sniper as proposed (I32): supply is the limit, not money, so $900 and $5k give the same answer. The clean pool was $205 over 47 days for everyone arriving 10 s or later, $4.40 a day in total. If we got half at 10 to 30 s: about $2 a day, and nothing on days with no release. The part-way pool is $2,450 / 47 = $52 a day for all late arrivers, lumpy (three movies = 75%). Nobody has shown RT triggers it, and a scraper does not know those outcomes. Even if RT does trigger it and we took a third, it would be about $15 a day in release weeks. That is NOT measured, and the one-second sweepers above lost 5 of 12. Honest figure: $0 to 2 a day at either bank size.

Spin-off 'follow the jump', NOT measured live: about 1.8 jumps a day. At $900, 100 contracts × about 7c (the +6c-cost row) × 1.8 = about $13 a day, with about $58 a jump held for up to 5 days (about $500 tied up). At $5k, 500 contracts = about $60 a day, if the order book is deep enough and the edge is real. The t of 1.73 at realistic cost means the true edge could be zero.
chk.worst_case: Buying into a jump that reverses. ONS-66 is the model: swept from 3c to 35c, settled NO. 100 contracts at about 25 to 50c loses $25 to $50 plus fee. Strikes of one movie move together, so 3 strikes × 100 contracts × 60c is about -$180 on one movie. A cached or misread RT page that buys the wrong side at 50 to 80c loses $50 to $80 per 100 contracts. Spin-off worst case: its 25 losing jumps in 82 would each lose the full entry, about 58c × size.
chk.killer_risks: (1) The speed race is already lost. 56% of the cheap volume left after the move went in the first second to one sweeper, and 44% of jumps were over within 1 s. A 10 to 30 s poller arrives after that. (2) The clean prize, where the score crosses the line and the result is nearly certain, was only $205 in 47 days for all late arrivers combined. (3) The biggest 'stale' farmer quotes were RIGHT. The two largest sweeps lost, so 'stale' in the original tally was a hindsight label. (4) RT may not be the trigger. We cannot check it historically: the review API needs a login, and review dates are day-only. The fastest sweepers being right only 7 of 12 times suggests they react to something less exact than the RT count. (5) The RT page is cached for 88 to 120 s. Getting around it means cache-busting, which anyone can do, and RT's terms of use likely ban scraping, so a fast poller risks an IP block. (6) Small sample: 18 movies, lumpy, three movies carry most of the money. (7) Spin-off: tape-only, not significant at realistic spread cost (t 1.73), and 1 of 2 entry times tried was picked.

chk.measured:
BOTTOM LINE: The idea as proposed (let the fastest bots go first and take what is left 3 s or more later) is dead. The "$400/week left after the first bots" was mostly a timestamp error. Once that is corrected, what is left is about $2-8 a day, shared by EVERY slow taker. The only real money is in the first second after a posting, and that is a speed race nobody has measured us in.

1) Where the $400/week came from. Script: sweep/check-I33/fine.py, realign.py, realign2.py (outputs *.out). Source: whlag_raw.jsonl.gz, which covers 10 settled KXTRUMPACT weeks (JUL12 to SEP13): 23 bursts of postings, 48 strikes locked YES. Taking the whitehouse.gov time as the lock time, as the idea did, taker YES buys at 97c or less printed 10-300 s after the lock total $4,139 gross. That matches the claimed ~$400/week.

But 8 of the 48 strikes carry hand-set times ending in :00. On 09-08 five items are all stamped 22:50:00Z, and the prices show they actually appeared one by one over about 4 minutes:
- T7 traded at 19c, then 62c, and was only swept to 96-98c at +239 s.
- T8 traded at 10c at +89 s and was swept at +246-254 s.

That one burst was 60% of all the money left at +2 s or later. Re-anchored on the real moment a bot swept each strike:
- Left for everyone after the first bot plus 2 s: about $577 gross in 10 weeks. That is $58/week, about $8/day for all takers combined.
- After +10 s: $267 gross, about $4/day for all takers.
- A strict anchor (the first buy at 97c or more) gives $135 net in 10 weeks at +2 s, about $1.90/day.
- 67% of the +2 s money came from ONE week (SEP13 T9/T10, $389). In the median burst, $0 is left after +2 s.

2) The first second is where the money is. Money taken inside the first second after a lock: $2,331 net in 10 weeks with the strict anchor ($33/day). Using the first-bot-reaction anchor and dropping the hand-stamped bursts, the first 2 s hold about $5,900 gross ($85/day). Either way it goes to whoever is first, and it is usually one bot clearing the whole sell side at once. For example, it bought SEP13 T10 all the way from 19c to 75c within one second.

3) How fast the incumbent bot is. Of 37 strikes with real (not hand-set) times, the first trade printed in the same second as the posting time 10 times and one second later about 22 times.

4) How fast we are, measured today from this laptop (latency.py, racewatch.py):
- The cache-busted feed missed the cache 8 of 8 times, so we read the live page.
- Full feed fetch: 0.62 s median (625 KB). An "unchanged" check (304 reply): 0.32 s, or 0.405 s median over 43 polls inside the watcher.
- Kalshi round trip: 0.08-0.12 s.
- Polling once a second, our order would land about 0.7-1.7 s after an item goes live. That is the same speed class as the incumbent, not clearly faster.

5) The rest of the family (family.py, last 8 settled events each, 112 GETs). Money printed 2-300 s after the lock sweep:
- KXEOWEEK: $148 net in 8 weeks, about $2.60/day for everyone. Its rule counts executive orders by signing date (Federal Register), so a White House posting is a proxy, not a lock.
- KXTRUMPENDORSEMENTS: $6 in 8 weeks.
- KXTRUMPPHOTO and KXTRUTHSOCIAL: no lock sweep at all. Their counts creep up, so there is never a stale-offer moment.

6) This week right now (live_book.py, thisweek.py, racewatch baseline):
- KXTRUMPACT-26SEP20 count is 0 so far. The watcher confirms 0 items dated Sep 20 or later.
- T1 is offered at 97c: $63 of profit sits at 97c or less if it locks.
- T2 is offered at 90c: $186 of profit.

- The T1/T2 trades this week show no sign of an item being posted and then pulled.
- Fees: quadratic, multiplier 1, on all five series.

Everything above is the trade tape (what other people took), not our fills. Checks at the end of the job: collector and crypto feeds alive, no script of mine left running, 87.8 GB free disk.
chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
SECOND WAVE ONLY (the idea as written). Everyone who is 2 s or more late shares about $1.90-8/day (all takers, 10-week average, net of the taker fee 0.07·p·(1-p) ≈ 1c a contract at 80c). If we took half of it: about $1-4/day. It is lumpy. Two thirds came from one week, and most weeks leave $0-15. The amount is capped by how many cheap offers there are, not by our bank, so it is the same at $900 and at $5,000. Money sits tied up until the Sunday 14:00Z close, 2-6 days after a lock, and at $900 that competes with pinrun's bank.

FIRST WAVE (only if we win the race; NOT measured). All takers together share $33-85/day, and one IOC order takes the whole sell side. A single sweep costs $1-5k, so a $900 bank captures only part of it. Illustration only: winning 1 burst in 4 at $900 would be roughly $5-20/day, and at $5k roughly $8-30/day. How often we would win is unknown.
chk.worst_case: We buy a strike at 70-97c and the item behind it is pulled, or re-dated into another week, before Kalshi's check at 10:00 AM ET Sunday. We lose the whole stake on that strike. Capped at $150 per burst that is -$150; uncapped at the $900 bank it is about -$900. It was not seen in 10 weeks (the count matched settlement 10 of 10), but hand-set timestamps (8 of 48 strikes) show the White House does edit dates. Also possible: a parser counts an item dated in a different week, which is guarded by counting by displayed ET date. Losing the race itself costs nothing: an IOC order at 97c or less simply goes unfilled.
chk.killer_risks:
1) The incumbent bot already prints within 0-1 s of the posting time and clears the whole sell side at once. Our measured detect-plus-order time at a 1-second poll is 0.7-1.7 s, so we may lose almost every race. Money left after +2 s is about $1.90-8/day for all takers combined.

2) The evidence was mostly a timestamp error. The White House hand-stamps some batches (five items at 22:50:00), and those batches produced the fake "slow money" in the second wave.

3) Polling harder to win (4 or more requests a second) risks getting blocked. whitehouse.gov already returns 403 on its WordPress JSON API.

4) Money is locked until Sunday. At $900 that starves pinrun.

5) Settlement risk from pulled or re-dated items; see worst case.

6) KXEOWEEK counts orders by signing date, so a White House post does not really lock it.

7) KXTRUMPPHOTO and KXTRUTHSOCIAL have no lock moment at all, so they add nothing.

ref.strongest_objection:
Most of the money comes from two days. Three strikes on those two days produced 73% of all the money (after fees) that takers made in 10 weeks: SEP13-T10 $1,715, SEP13-T9 $1,425 (both 09-18) and JUL19-T10 $1,401 (07-23), together $4,540 of $6,194. On those days the White House posted a 9th or 10th action that the market had priced at 19-46c. Two such days in 70 cannot tell us how often they happen: the plausible range runs from about 0.2 to 7 such days per 10 weeks. Leave those three strikes out and a bot like ours makes about $2-6 a day even when it wins the race.

Those days are also decided by fractions of a second among 3 to 6 bots. The same bots were buying 1.2-1.7 s after each posting. The fastest one looks like a once-a-second poller, and it could cut half a second at almost no cost the first time it loses a $600 event. If it gets 0.4 s faster, our simulated take falls by about a third.

Two things I could not test:
- Blocking: nobody has tested whether whitehouse.gov blocks about 10,800 cache-busted requests an hour for hours at a time. My 40-second test at 3 requests a second got 97 replies and no blocks.
- Pulled or re-dated items: whether a posted item is ever deleted or re-dated before the Sunday 10:00 AM ET check. The Internet Archive was down ("Temporarily Offline"), so I could not look for items that disappeared. A false lock on a 19c strike loses the whole stake. The feed's lastBuildDate (Tue 22 Sep 22:08:33Z) shows at least one of its 30 items was edited after it was posted; I could not tell what changed.

I found nothing that kills the fast (first-in-line) version. The idea as written is dead: it lets the fast bots go first and takes what is left 3 s or more later, and that pays under $8 a day for all slow takers combined.

Scripts and outputs are in C:/Users/Joe/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--kals-repo/47b37ac1-655c-4d72-a81b-a48e9625d5bd/scratchpad/sweep/refute-I33/ (subsec.py, curve.py, mc2_tail.py, prepub.py, lat.py, keepalive.py, rules.py, wayback.py and their .out files). I used 57 Kalshi GETs and about 140 whitehouse.gov requests.

1) Kalshi trade times carry microseconds, and the checker cut them to whole seconds. I re-pulled every YES-locked KXTRUMPACT strike from JUL12 to SEP13. For each one I took the White House posting second (the <time datetime> on list pages 1-8, 80 items) and measured when the first YES buy printed after it.

ref.revised_dollars_per_day:
The idea as written, taking what is left 3 s or more after a posting, pays $8 a day for all slow takers combined, so our share is under $1-4 a day. That part is dead.

The fast version is still possible. We would poll 3 times a second on a connection kept open, read only the start of the feed, and send the order about 0.3 s after spotting a new item. My simulation says about $8 a day with a $150 cap per strike and about $22 a day with $400. These figures lean high, and 75% of them comes from 2 days in 10 weeks. Realistically that is $3-12 a day on average, but lumpy: most weeks pay $0, and one surprise week pays about $300-700.

To confirm it, change racewatch.py to use a kept-open connection at about 3 requests a second instead of starting curl once a second. Then log our detection time against the first buy on Kalshi. Pass bar: across 6 or more locks, we detect before the first buy in at least half of them.

chk.measured:
SHORT VERSION: the idea as written is dead. The morning version is not proven, and on its one live day it would have lost money.

1) LIVE TEST, 2026-09-25 (read-only logger rcplog.py). It checked RCP's data file every 10 s past the CDN cache, and saved Kalshi books at +0/5/15/30/60 s whenever the number changed.
- Change 1 (Rasmussen, 38.8 -> 38.9). RCP's internal build was 10:41:47 ET. Kalshi reacted 7 s later but only partly: E38.9 went from 27c to 40c, then fell back to 21-35c. The data file went public at 10:47:59 ET and we saw it at 10:48:04. The book at that moment had 3,205 E38.9 YES contracts offered at 30-45c. The market did not commit until a sweep at 11:38:12 ET, 50 minutes after we saw the change. Takers bought 7,196 E38.9 YES at 33-67c in that gap.
- Change 2 (RMG, 38.9 -> 38.8). Build was 12:01:46 ET. E38.8 was swept from 17c to 95c by 12:02:05, and one buyer came in 4 s before the build stamp. The file went public at 12:07:56 and we saw it at 12:08:04, six minutes after the market had finished repricing. E38.8 was at 94c by then.
- 1 PM settlement: 38.8, E38.8 YES. The file's latest value matched settlement (1 of 1).
- Paper result at a $300 cap, holding to settlement: buy about 830 E38.9 at about 36c on change 1 = -$300. Buy E38.8 at 94c on change 2 = +$18. Net about -$282.
- Round-trip version: only about 275 contracts of bids at about 76c were hit before 12:01. On those, +$100 to +$112. Depth beyond that was not measured.

idea.name: Brazil election-night count-order projection (Oct 4, runoff Oct 25)
idea.family: foreign elections x official TSE results JSON
idea.mechanism: Poll TSE's national and per-state JSON (resultados.tse.jus.br) every 10-30 s on election night. Project final shares from the partial count weighting each state/municipality by its 2022 turnout and result and by what is uncounted. When the running tally misleads (in 2022 Bolsonaro led until ~70% counted; final Lula 48.4 vs 43.3), buy the side the projection favours on first-round-winner, margin, outright-win and vote-share ladders. Also record Kalshi and TSE live even if not trading.
idea.why_mispriced: Retail traders read the headline running tally while the Lula-leaning Northeast reports late.
idea.must_be_true: Count order in 2026 is again regionally skewed, our projection beats other bots that know the 2022 pattern, and Kalshi keeps markets open until the media call.
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: One-off $0-400 per election night (2 nights); ~$0-10/day amortized; speculative.
idea.data_needed: Backtest the projection on 2022 per-state/municipality results plus any archived minute-by-minute 2022 snapshots (journalists' GitHub scrapes).
idea.evidence_so_far: TSE 2022 national file returns HTTP 200; 2026 config not published. Books: KXBRPRES1R Lula 73-75c (24h volume 12k; OI 28k Lula / 44k Flavio); KXVOTEBR1 45 markets with 10-60c spreads; polymarket.com first-round Lula 73-74c. Analog: Michigan Dem Senate primary margin bracket went 1c -> 32c -> 92c over 4.5 h with ~$500k of true-side buying at <= 95c (and about as much wrong-side).

These are estimates, not measurements. At most 2 nights: round 1 on Oct 4 and the runoff on Oct 25. Polls close at 4:00 pm ET both nights.

$900 bank:

- That gives about $20-45 expected per night, $40-90 in total, or about $0.10-0.25 a day spread over a year.

$5k bank:
- $500-1,000 a night, mainly in KXBRPRES on runoff night (2.6M contracts open, so the book can absorb it).
- About $100-400 if the mis-price happens, about $30-150 expected per night, or about $0.20-0.80 a day over a year.

chk.worst_case:
If the projection is wrong (the count order changes in 2026, or Flavio genuinely wins), the whole stake is lost on that night: -$100 at the $900 bank, -$500 to -$1,000 at $5k. Every Brazil position that night rides the same count, so spreading across markets does not help. If the 2022 pattern breaks, both nights can lose: -$200 at $900. The idea's proposed $150-300 stake is 17-33% of the $900 bank, which is too much for an all-or-nothing, never-tested bet.

Money can also be tied up. Kalshi held Peru's first-round market open for 33 days waiting for the official result. Colombia's closed the next morning. Brazil's vote-share and margin markets wait for certified results, possibly weeks, which takes that money away from pinrun.
chk.killer_risks:
1) The late Northeast comeback was national news in 2014 and 2022. Polymarket's international site has $155M on this election, and Kalshi tracks it within a cent (first-round Lula 73-74c on both). If the crowd already prices the projection, there is zero edge and we pay fees and spread.
2) The count order may not repeat. Transmission order, Northeast turnout, or where Flavio is strong compared with Jair could differ. A projection trained on 2022 then confidently buys the loser.
3) Projection accuracy at a partial count is unmeasured. With a 2-4 point race, the error at 50% counted may be 1-2 points, so the projection is least sure exactly when prices are cheapest.
4) Access: cdn.tse.jus.br already returns 403 from this box. The results site works today, but blocking of foreign traffic or rate limits on election night could leave the bot blind.
5) n = 2 nights, so nothing statistical can ever be concluded. Every analog 'pot' above is hindsight on other people's trades, not our fills.
6) The only analog that clearly worked (Peru 2nd place) ran over a slow, 11-hour count. Brazil's count finishes in about 3 hours, and the Colombia fast count repriced within about 60 minutes.

ref.strongest_objection:
The checker's main money scenario doesn't show up in any of the four past count nights I could check. That scenario: the crowd follows the misleading running count, and we buy the side our projection favours at about 40c when it really wins about 85% of the time. What the order books actually show:

1) When the count-order pattern was already well known, the crowd did not panic. In Moldova's Nov 3, 2024 runoff, everyone knew from two weeks earlier that votes from Moldovans abroad come in last. Sandu trailed the running count from polls closing (2:00 pm ET) until 4:13 pm ET. Her Polymarket price never fell below 78c: 82c before the count, 83-85c while she trailed, and 96c at 3:27 pm ET, 45 minutes before she took the lead in the count. In Moldova's 2025 parliamentary election, the pro-EU party (PAS) never fell below 91c. Brazil's late comeback is at least as well known (2014 and 2022).

2) The big dips happened only in razor-thin races, where no projection could honestly have claimed much more than a coin flip:
- Moldova's 2024 EU referendum was the first time the pattern showed up. Yes fell from 97c to 6c and still won, 50.35% to 49.65%.
- Peru's 2026 second-place race: the Lima-backed candidate traded at 82-92c for about 11 hours, on Kalshi and on Polymarket ($2.0M traded there). He lost second place by 0.13 points.

So the money is either a lag of roughly 10c in a clear race, or a long-shot bet on a near coin flip in a razor-thin one. Two nights can never show which. And the checker's own trigger (projection at least 90% sure and price at or below 75c) would have fired on none of these four nights. It could fire in Brazil round 1 only because Lula starts at 73c.

3) The count pattern itself is not stable. I downloaded TSE's official 2022 count history; it is not blocked, see checks. The gap between the running margin and the final margin was 9.6 points at about 26% counted in round 1, but 3.9 points at about 29% counted in round 2. That is the same candidates four weeks apart. The file is national-only: no per-state rows in 8,437 round-1 rows or 5,286 round-2 rows. So the per-state backtest in the checker's next test cannot be built from the official file.

None of this makes the idea lose money on average. It is a coin-flip-style bet on a hard-to-model projection, with no way to confirm it beforehand.

1) THE RULE QUESTION IS SETTLED (rules.out, from market rules_secondary). KXDHOUSEWON and KXRHOUSEWON count "only the regular general election in each of the 435 congressional districts ... No district counts twice." Every district goes to one winner: by the 4-of-8 media-call test, or else by state certification. So the 6 non-voting delegates do not count, and D + R can never exceed 435. Buying NO on "D>=214" and NO on "R>=222" really does pay at least $1. The only way both lose is a single winner recorded on BOTH the Democratic and Republican ballot lines (the rule accepts "any one of several ballot lines"), and the result also landing exactly on the 214/222 boundary. I did not measure that probability; I judge it well under 1 in 1,000.

2) THE PACKAGE IS REAL AND IT STAYS. Books in books.json and excl.out, re-checked at 13:13Z with house_pair_recheck.py. D>=214 has a YES bid of 96c for 2,687 contracts, then 95c for 700. R>=222 has a YES bid of 6c for 11,648. Pair cost is 98c plus 0.66c taker fee = 98.66c. That locks +1.34c per pair on 2,687 pairs and +0.27c on 700 more. Total: 3,387 pairs, +$37.82, on $3,349 of capital. The gap was also present at about 08:30Z (the earlier scout run), so it has lasted at least 4.7 hours. It is the ONLY profitable pair.

- Artefact checks passed: the book price unit matches the independent yes_bid_dollars field on /markets (0.96 and 0.06); the book side is right (NO ask = 1 - YES bid); the fee multiplier is 1 (series read).

3) THE CAPITAL IS LOCKED UNTIL FEB 1, 2027, NOT ELECTION NIGHT. The markets close 2027-01-03 and expire 2027-02-01, and the rule counts calls "as they stand at the Expiration time". Every comparable 2024 market also settled at Feb 1, 2025 15:00Z despite can_close_early=True (/historical/markets: CONTROLH-2024, CONTROLS-2024, RHOUSESEATS-25, RSENATESEATS-25; hist_markets.out). So it is about 129 days. Kalshi pays 3.25% APY on cash AND open positions (help.kalshi.com APY page, $250 minimum balance), so the lock costs no interest. The +1.13% is excess return, about 3.2% a year.

4) 2024 CALL-LAG AND LATE-SETTLEMENT EVIDENCE. Source: Kalshi's own hourly candles from /historical/markets/{t}/candlesticks, Nov 5, 2024 to Feb 1, 2025 (candles2024.json, daily2024.out). This is market trade data, not a replay.

idea.name: Company KPI release sweep (markets stay open after the press release)

ref.strongest_objection:
The checker's money case assumed we could place orders within 10 seconds of the release. I timed today the free sources a laptop could use, and none of them is that fast:
- **EDGAR current-filings feed:** a new filing shows up 13 to 51 seconds after the SEC accepts it (median 31, 12 filings).
- **data.sec.gov submissions API:** 32 to 91 seconds (median 50, 18 filings). The SEC says this is "typically under 1 second"; that is not what a laptop sees.
- **PR Newswire free RSS:** releases appear 56 to 145 seconds after their stamped minute (median 116). The 10:00 AM ET releases showed up about 2 minutes late.
- **Business Wire public RSS:** its cache header allows copies up to 5 minutes old (s-maxage=300), and it did not update once in 11 minutes. It is not usable.

The existing sweepers already sit at the free-EDGAR speed. On the events where they fired after the filing, they fired 22 to 35 seconds after it on five of them (GOOG +22 s, ABNB +28, LUV +33/+35, MCD +34, WING +29). At best we would tie them.

Where the money was, across 55 events, re-derived with my own queries:
- About two-thirds of the winning-side money below 97c ($11.6k) was taken before the company's 8-K or 6-K even reached EDGAR. Only a newswire or company website could have reached it, and on most events the sweepers there fire 0.1 to 11 seconds after release.

- Clean, undisputed money a free-EDGAR bot could have reached was about $0.5k for the season, and $344 of that is one event (Chewy).

What is still unmeasured is scraping each company's investor-relations page. The slow sweepers that bought before the filing reached EDGAR (AMZN at +51 s after the wire, MCD at about +34 s, NCLH at about +44 s) could in principle be beaten that way. That is now the only open route.

Smaller risks:
- Kalshi Rule 5.10 lets Kalshi cancel trades done more than 20c away from fair value when an order was placed in error. Sweeps at 32c after the release fall in that zone. Kalshi says this happens only in "extraordinary circumstances", so it is a tail risk.
- The contract lists the press release first among its sources and marks the market "can close early". So a release that comes out rounded or with an adjusted definition (Match exactly on its 13.25M strike; Robinhood "28.4M", "4.8M") is the settlement value. idea.name: Fear & Greed 4 PM snapshot (KXFEAR)
idea.family: financials / index on a public page
idea.mechanism: KXFEAR settles on CNN's Fear & Greed category 'at 4:00 PM ET' on Fridays but stays open 6 min to 23 h after 4 PM. CNN's public JSON (production.dataviz.cnn.io/index/fearandgreed/graphdata) gives the score and its 7 components with timestamps, updated after the close (S&P ~20:36Z, put/call ~21:06Z, breadth/strength 23:59Z).
