What kills it: all three pieces together would earn at most about $5-20 in total, one time, while tying up about $350 of cash until Jan 1, 2027. The same cash in the live bot earns roughly $2.50 a day per $100. And taking that much cash out would trip the live bot's 20% drawdown stop, because the bot measures its bank from cash alone.

Sources: order books pulled read-only at about 10:05 AM ET on 09-25 (337 requests, 31 long-dated crypto series), plus trade history for 8 markets (21 more requests). Files are in C:/Users/Joe/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--kals-repo/47b37ac1-655c-4d72-a81b-a48e9625d5bd/scratchpad/sweep/check-I50/ (snap.json, scan.out, scan2.out, tr_an.out, trades_*.json). Prices at the time: BTC $83,547, ETH $2,686, SOL $119.46, taken from the 15-minute market strikes.

(a) The two "BTC above $100k" markets are now the same price. KXBTCMAX100-26-DEC is 38c bid / 39c ask, and KXBTCMAXY-99999.99 is also 38/39. The 4c gap in the morning snapshot is gone. Over 30 days of trades (189k and 147k contracts), the hour-by-hour price gap was 0.0c at the median and ran from -3.1c to +3.3c (5th to 95th percentile), drifting back and forth over days. For a gap to pay when buying both sides outright, the higher bid must beat the lower ask by more than about 3.4c (two taker fees of ~1.7c each), which almost never happens. With one side resting as a maker order, it pays about 0.5-2c per pair, and only in the ~15-20% of hours when the gap is 2c or more. Whether our resting order would actually fill is not measured.

(b) SOL: the pairing the idea named (touch $150 at 40c + ends above $149.99 sold at 31c) costs 112c for a guaranteed 100c, so it can lose 12c per package. It is not safe. The real near-safe version found here is different: buy "SOL touches $180" at 20c and sell "SOL ends above $199.99" at 22c. If SOL finishes above $200 it must have touched $180, so the package always pays at least $1, plus a second $1 if SOL touches $180 but finishes below $200. Working through the whole SOL book at every strike: 343 packages, $348 of cash, worst case -$5.22 (fees). Expected profit is +$4.61 using a deliberately cautious estimate, or +$19.65 using the standard rule of thumb that the chance of ending above a level is about half the chance of touching it. The high bids that make this work are a this-week event. On the $199.99 market, people selling into bids at 18c or higher moved 795 contracts in the last week, against 0, 21, 0 and 3 in the four weeks before, so other traders are already taking them. On the $149.99 market the same count was 500, 26, 170 and 78 contracts by week.

(c) ETH year-end brackets (no fee on this series; the 18 brackets cover every price with no gaps): a full set that pays exactly $1 costs 97.3c for 1 set, 97.6c for 10, 98.3c for 25, 98.8c for 50, 99.2c for 100 and 100.4c for 250. The most profit on offer is about $0.80 in total. A full set of the BTC year-end brackets costs $1.013 to $1.030, so it loses money.

Other pairs where one market must always pay at least as much as another (BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL touch vs end-of-year, and higher vs lower touch levels): all are at or past break-even after fees except the SOL case above. (My scan listed the Sept and Oct BTC $100k markets as "locked +20c", but that is a bug. Those markets close before Jan 1, so the pairing does not hold.)

Things checked that could have made a good number false. The SOL touch market's window runs to midnight Jan 1 and includes the last minute, so the "always pays $1" logic holds with a $20 cushion. Kalshi pays 3.25% a year on cash AND on open positions (help center, balances of $250 or more), so locking cash does not lose the interest. But pinrun.py read_bank() uses cash only: size_for_bank sizes the bot from cash, and drawdown() compares cash to the high-water mark. Buying $348 of positions at a $1,043 bank reads as a 33% drawdown, which halts the bot, and cuts its size from 88 to about 58.
chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
At the $900 bank this loses money overall. Best case: SOL +$4.6 to +$19.7 expected over the ~98 days to Jan 1, which is $0.05-0.20 a day. The BTC pair, with about $100-300 committed, would make about $1-6 over the same 98 days, or $0.01-0.06 a day, if resting orders fill at all. ETH sets: under $0.80 in total. What that cash costs instead: the live bot has made +$437.82 over the ~17 days since 09-08 (Kalshi's ledger), about $26 a day at size 88 with a $1,043 bank. That is roughly $2.50 a day per $100 of cash. $348 locked therefore costs about $8.70 a day in lost bot size, and it trips the 20% drawdown halt outright. Net: about -$8 a day, or worse while the bot is halted.

At a $5k bank: the bot tops out at size 250, which needs about 250 x $11.85 = ~$2,960. That leaves about $2,000 of cash idle, which could fund this without shrinking the bot. The total would be SOL ~$5-20 once, BTC pair ~$15-23 per 98 days on $1,000 if fills happen (not measured), and ETH under $1. That is about $0.2-0.4 a day, and only after pinrun's bank and drawdown logic is changed to count position value. Otherwise $1,000 of positions against a $5k high-water mark reads as a 20% drawdown and halts the bot.
chk.worst_case: The worst case is not the trades themselves. It is the live bot halting: buying about $210 or more of long-dated positions at the current ~$1,043 bank drops cash past the 20% drawdown stop, and every halted day costs about $26 of the bot's average profit. On the trades alone, at the full ~343 SOL packages: -$5.22 after fees, even if SOL goes to $500. BTC pair: -$1 per pair only in the near-impossible case that the two markets settle differently (BTC first crossing $100k in the final minute of 2026, or landing exactly on $100,000.00). Plus 1-3c per pair if the resting side fills and the price of the other side moves before we can buy it. ETH sets: -$1 per set only if the year-end price lands inside a 1-cent gap between brackets, about 1 chance in 10,000.
chk.killer_risks: 1) Too small: the whole thing is a one-time $5-20 expected profit on about $348 of cash, not a steady stream. The high SOL bids showed up this week (795 contracts) after about 0-21 contracts a week before, and other traders are already selling into them. 2) Cash is locked until Jan 1, 2027. Kalshi still pays 3.25% interest on it, but at $900 the bot needs every dollar: it earns about $2.50 a day per $100, this earns about $0.05. 3) The live bot sizes itself and triggers its 20% drawdown stop from CASH only (pinrun.py read_bank / size_for_bank / drawdown), so buying positions on the same account shrinks it and can halt it. That needs a versioned live code change before any hold-to-January trade. 4) The BTC $100k gap has already closed (both 38/39). DATA: 683 MLB games, 2026-08-04 to 09-25. Kalshi KXMLBGAME settled markets (2 GETs), 1-minute candles for both team markets from the 5th inning to the final out (85 GETs), and Kalshi trades for 80 random games (288 GETs). Game states come from the public MLB statsapi play-by-play. The reference is a win-expectancy table built from 8,973 games (2023-2025, plus 2026 before 08-04), so it contains none of the test games. Sanity check: outcome minus table on the test games was -0.02c (se 1.16), so the table fits this season. Taker fee: KXMLBGAME multiplier is 0.5, so 0.035*p*(1-p). Every number below is clustered by game.

1) "STEP-LIKE LATE CALIBRATION" (Moshrefi) IS A LOOK-AHEAD ARTEFACT (a window defined by information from the future). Same 520 games, favourite bought at the taker price once a minute:
- Window "last 10 min before the final out" (needs the future): the favourite looks underpriced. +2.04c/contract at 97-99c (t 6.5), +5.16c at 90-95c (t 5.0), +8.97c at 75-90c.
- Window "every minute from the top of the 9th to the final out" (knowable live), same games: +0.50c (se 0.96) at 97-99c, -1.18c at 90-95c, -5.45c at 75-90c (t -1.7).
- Why: comebacks make games longer, so they fall out of "the final 10 minutes". The paper's effect is exactly this.

2) BUY THE LEADER AT INNING BREAKS (score frozen about 2 min, so a slow feed is fine). 5,002 break states, 680 games:
- Leader midpoint vs the table: +0.17c (se 0.15). The market is calibrated.
- Buying the leader at the taker price, all bands: -0.72c/contract (se 1.13).
- Best band 97-99c: +0.58c (se 0.75, t 0.8), but the table says -0.46c for that same band.
- Mirror, buying the longshot: 0-3c loses -1.11c (t -1.8), 3-5c loses -1.96c (t -2.8). Against the table the longshot is only +0.42c / +0.45c overpriced, which is about half the 1c spread (median spread 1c).
- Nothing survives the half-spread plus fee. Kills the taker leg.

3) MAKER LONGSHOT SELLER (the only live thread). 80 games, 77,831 fills, 23.0M contracts of takers buying the longshot at 5c or less. Median 128k contracts per game at 2-4c, all takers, all queue positions.
- Markout = the sell price minus the longshot's midpoint 60 seconds later; positive means the sale looks good a minute on. A no-fill clock-grid comparison drifts -0.01c.

- When the level CLEARED (what a late joiner at the back of a deep 1c queue gets): -0.93c (se 0.44) and -0.75c (se 0.15).

(2) The only "edge" left is the 1c spread. The midpoint is calibrated to the out-of-sample table within 0.17c (se 0.15), so there is no mispricing to harvest, only spread to earn by making.

How it works:
- Subscribe read-only via WebSocket to orderbook_delta and trade for the live KXMLBGAME tickers (REST polling of 30 books would burst the shared rate limit).
- Poll statsapi /game/{pk}/feed/live for the game state.
- Place a virtual resting longshot sell (a NO bid at 95-98c) the moment a new best level forms, only while the lead is 3 or more in the 7th inning or later.
- Track the queue ahead of us from deltas and trades.
- Cancel virtually on any baserunner or scoring event, using the feed's own timestamp.
- Log each virtual fill with the midpoint 60 s and 600 s later, plus the final result.

Pass bar, written before any look:
- At least 40 games with fills, clustered by game.
- Virtual fills of at least 200 contracts/game.
- 60-s markout of +0.30c/contract or better after the maker fee, with t of at least 2.
- Level-cleared fills making up no more than 30% of our contracts.

Fail on any one: kill I51 entirely.

Separately, the taker legs need no further test. They are dead on 680 games.

ref.strongest_objection:
The only money in this idea is the 1c gap between the buy price and the sell price. That gap goes to whoever is first in line at a price and quickest to pull their order, which is professional market makers, not a laptop bot. I could not show the sign is negative for us, but three measured facts point that way.

(1) The free MLB live feed is slow. Measured live today on 142 pitches of the CHC@BOS game, it showed each pitch 14 s late (median), 8.6 s with cache-busting, and about 8.8 s for balls in play. In past games, 26 of every 100 price jumps after a trailing-team baserunner happened within 5 s, and 40 within 10 s. So "cancel when the feed shows a baserunner" is too late about 4 times in 10.

(2) An order left resting at 2-4c in the 7th inning or later gets run over (the price moves through it) in about 17 of every 100 minutes. Each time it loses 1.1c a contract, and the loss is still there 5 minutes later. A normal fill earns about +0.8c, so the bot breaks even only if at least ~57% of its fills are normal ones. The market as a whole gets ~89% normal, but the last order in line absorbs the run-overs first.

(3) Our place in line cannot be measured from REST snapshots. The displayed size at the best price swings 2-5x within seconds. Two Kalshi endpoints read no more than 8 s apart agreed on the best price only 29 times out of 57.

Two costs on top of that:
- The ceiling is small. One comeback loses 97c a contract, so size is capped at about 60-120 contracts a game on the $900 bank. That is roughly $0.3-1 a game even when everything works.
- It shares cash with pinrun. pinrun sizes itself from the cash balance every 5 minutes and counts any unexplained cash move over $1 as a deposit or withdrawal (EXTERNAL_MIN = 1.00). Money locked in evening games (7 pm-1 am ET) therefore shrinks the live bot's size unless pinrun is changed.

What I could NOT refute: sellers of late-game longshots as a group do get paid, in both MLB and NFL.

Needed before any money: the checker's paper test must run on Kalshi's WebSocket order-book deltas, not snapshots. The cancel must be driven by Kalshi's own book moving, not by the MLB feed. Pass bar: at least ~60% normal fills and a +0.3c/contract markout after fees on at least 40 games.

idea.name: Mention markets: NO-side fades (pre-event YES overpricing, in-event late NO, transcript base rates)
idea.family: mentions / calibration
idea.mechanism: (a) Three hours before the event ends buy NO at (1 - yes_bid) on every word whose YES mid is 10-65c; during the event an ASR (I31) sells a NO leg within 1-3 s of the word being said. (b) During the event buy NO at 90-98c on words not yet said and hold. (c) Price each word from the speaker's historical frequency in public transcripts (Factba.se, earnings transcripts) and buy NO where the YES ask exceeds the base rate by >= 5c.
idea.why_mispriced: Fans and retail buy YES on catchphrases and fun words; hopeful YES holders late in the event.
idea.must_be_true: The YES overpricing exists out of sample -- it FAILED its pre-registered holdout; late in-event NO at 90-98c is roughly fair on the candles; base rates are stable and early-close mechanics handled.
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: $0-10/day for (a) only with ASR exits and a forward test; ~$0 for (b); $0-3/day for (c).
idea.data_needed: Forward paper test over 15-20 Trump events against the bar in holdout_prereg.txt; transcript base-rate table for 30 events.
idea.evidence_so_far: Fade: recent live-window sample, 32 Trump events (Jul 22-Sep 24): +7.70c/contract per event (t 3.13); pooled +6.15c, 9.2% on cost, 22 events positive / 10 negative. PRE-REGISTERED HOLDOUT (11 older events, 2025-04..2026-06 via /historical): -7.79c/contract, t -0.99, MDE 16c -> FAIL. Other speakers: 45 events +1.3c (t 0.32); earnings calls 18 events +4.0c (t 0.92). Late NO (1-minute candles, 40 Trump events) 60 min before end: NO at 90-95c won 92.75% (avg 91.9c, 69 words); 95-98c won 95.74% (avg 96.0c, 47 words): about fair; closer to the end 5-27 words, all won. Mentions at 24 h, YES 5-10c: -4.5c/contract (109 obs / 31 events); tape: sellers of YES < 5c +2.0c on 60k contracts, only 3 events. Files: sweep/entertainment-mentions-companies/fade_yes.py, trump_candles.jsonl.gz, trump_hist.jsonl.gz, holdout_result.out, holdout_prereg.txt, late_no.py, trump_lateno.out; sweep/calibration-bias/.

- Shape of a typical event: median 16 words bought, average NO price 66.8c, 28% of bought words were said.
- Supply is NOT measured for Trump words: no Trump mention event is open today (books_now.out). Other mention books today (Fed/Warsh, NVDA) show about 100-150 contracts within 2c of the best YES bid per word, and they look like program market makers.

(b) LATE NO AT 90-98c: DEAD. The earlier late_no.py timed its buys against Kalshi's actual close, which comes after the speech ends and is unknown while the speech is live. That is look-ahead. My rerun starts the clock at the first word-said price jump, which a bot can see live (late_no_real.py, late_no_real.out; 24 of 40 events). Buying NO at 90-98c from then on: 339 words, 93.2% won, +0.40c a contract per event (t 0.27), pooled +0.12c. With the fee rounded up per order it is -0.40c. All of the profit sits in buys made 15-30 min before the close (+3.5c on 83 words); buys made more than 30 min before the close lost 1.0c on 255 words.

(b') NEW ANGLE, SNIPING AFTER THE SPEECH ENDS: tape only. The rules say markets close only "after the address concludes and the outcomes are verified". I pulled the last 75 min of trades for 5 recent events (endlag.py, 158 GETs, endlag_trades.jsonl.gz, endprofile.out). Each event has a collapse, 1-3 minutes when stale YES bids on unsaid words get hit:

- SEP21: about $1,800 in 3 min
- SEP22: about $140
- SEP18: about $80
- SEP24: already collapsed before my window started
Those bids are hit by YES holders getting out as well as by snipers. Our share is unmeasured, and it needs a livestream end-of-speech detector (idea I31).

(c) BASE RATES: not built. Commercial transcript-count tools already exist (Polymark.et Mention Market Analyzer, Odds Assist Pro's earnings-mentions tool, found by web search), so the market very likely prices base rates already.

chk.worst_case:
Worst event seen: -$6.64 per one-contract-per-word slot over 15 words, 11 of them said (holdout1). At 20 contracts a word that is -$133; at 50 a word, -$332.

Plausible worst: a long, rambling speech hits all ~16 words at about 67c. That is -$214 at 20 a word and -$536 at 50 a word. Speeches are independent of each other, but a run of 3-4 long ones in a week at 20 a word could lose about $400 against about $19 an event expected.
chk.killer_risks:
1. The edge may be a recent regime or plain noise. Two pre-registered holdouts failed (-7.8c and +3.9c at t 1.09). Out-of-sample events before April 2026 lost money, and the "since April" split was chosen after seeing the data.
2. Insiders. Web-search headlines report a CFTC probe of mention markets (NPR, 2026-08-13) and a probe of a White House teleprompter operator who bet on Trump's words (NPR, 2026-07-16). I did not read the articles; the fetch timed out. People who have seen the script buy YES on words that will be said, and a NO fader sells to exactly them. There is also product risk: rule changes or delisting.
3. Depth for Trump words is unmeasured. No event is open today, and the historical candle bid may have been a 1-contract order.
4. Swings are large relative to the edge: about 14c a contract per event against about +6c expected. It takes roughly 20-30 events to tell the two apart.
5. Timing is untested. The rule uses the actual close minus 3 h; a live bot has to work from the scheduled start, and Trump often starts late.
6. Resolution rules can bite: whether Q&A counts, plural and possessive forms, the "3+ times" variants. For (b'), a speech the bot thinks has ended can resume, for example with Q&A, and hit NO bought at 90-98c.
7. (c) base rates are already sold as commercial tools, so there is little left to gain there.
chk.next_test:
Paper watcher, read-only. For every KXTRUMPMENTION and KXTRUMPMENTIONB event, record each word's YES bid, ask and depth down to 5c below the best bid at 3 h and at 2 h before the scheduled start. Apply the exact rule (YES mid 10-65c, spread 10c or less, buy NO at 1 - YES bid, taker fee), then score at settlement.

Pass bar, written now before any data: at least 15 events; mean per event above +2c a contract with t above 1.5; pooled above +2c; and median depth within 2c of the best YES bid of at least 20 contracts a word. Anything else kills (a). At about 0.45 events a day that takes about 5 weeks.

Optional add-on for (b'): log each event's end time from the livestream (one ASR tap), or by hand for 5 events, plus 1-second books in the last 5 minutes. That measures how long stale YES bids at 2c or more survive after the speech ends. If they last under 5 s, drop (b').
chk.capital_needed: About $214 per event at 20 contracts a word (16 words x 67c), tied up 3-5 hours. About $535 at 50 a word. Events rarely overlap, so one event's worth of capital covers it.

ref.strongest_objection:
The "YES has been overpriced since April 2026" story, which is the whole basis of the checker's +6c a contract and $8.6 a day, does not hold up on fresh data. I pre-registered a test before reading any prices (refute-I52/prereg_regime.txt) and ran the identical fade rule on every KXTRUMPMENTION event from 2026-04-01 to 07-21 that nobody had used yet. That was 46 events, 32 of which had qualifying words (480 words). Result: -6.25c a contract per event (t -1.58), pooled -5.25c. 23 events lost and 9 won, so under the pre-registered bar the regime is REFUTED. At 20 contracts a word that is -$15.75 per event.

The checker's 13 "since April" holdout events (+6.7c) were a lucky subset of the same months. Across all 45 out-of-sample events since April the fade makes -2.51c (t -0.79). The only profitable stretch is Aug-Sep, and that is exactly the window where the idea was discovered (in-sample), so the positive number is just the rule fitting the data it was found on. Month by month: Apr -1.3c, May +0.1c, Jun +0.5c, Jul -4.7c, Aug +5.4c, Sep +12.3c (only 8 events).

Across all 90 Trump events measured by anyone (2025-10 to 2026-09-24) the rule makes -0.14c a contract (t -0.06), with 43 events up and 47 down. The smallest edge that sample could detect is 4.2c, so any edge large enough to matter would have shown up.

The other legs change nothing. (b) late NO was already dead on the checker's look-ahead-free rerun. (b') sniping after the speech ends is really idea I31 (live speech-to-text) and has no measured share for us. (c) base rates: commercial tools already exist.

All numbers here come from my own queries and code, in refute-I52/. Everything is a candle/tape population, not our own fills, which is acceptable for a taker rule that hits a resting bid, but depth is still unmeasured.

1. FRESH PRE-REGISTERED SAMPLE. pull_regime.py and pull_regime2.py used about 1,430 GETs: the /markets settled list, /historical/markets and per-market /historical candlesticks. That covers all 46 unused KXTRUMPMENTION events with at least 8 markets and a first close in [2026-04-01, 2026-07-22). 32 had qualifying words.
   - Scoring (fade_regime.py) used the identical rule: last hourly candle at or before first_close - 3h, YES mid 10-65c, spread 10c or less, buy NO at 1 - yes_bid, taker fee 0.07p(1-p).
   - Result: -6.25c (t -1.58), pooled -5.25c, +9/-23.
   - Other anchors: H=2 gives -1.68c, H=4 gives -2.28c, H=6 gives -2.24c. None is positive.
   - One deviation from the pre-registration: the GET cap bound on the first pass, which took events in time order (Apr 1-Jun 10: -10.06c, t -5.65, +1/-11). I then pulled the remainder (Jun 11-Jul 17: -3.96c, t -0.63), so the final sample is the whole pre-registered population with no selection.
2. COMBINED (combined.py, de-duplicated by event, 5 files):
   - All 90 events: -0.14c (t -0.06), pooled +0.60c.
   - Out-of-sample 61: -3.53c (t -1.28).
   - Since April, all 74: +1.22c (t 0.55).
   - Since April, out-of-sample 45: -2.51c.
   - In-sample 29: +7.01c (t 2.68), which reproduces the checker.
   - Trend over time: +1.73c a month (t 2.43), driven by the Aug-Sep in-sample events.
3. ANCHOR SWEEP (hsweep.py): the in-sample is positive at every anchor from 2 to 8 h before the close (+6.3 to +9.6c). Both holdouts sit near 0 at every anchor. So the result is a property of the discovery period, not of the 3 h anchor.
4. DATA CHECK (candle_qc.py): the historical candles are continuous hourly, like the live ones. The snapshot candle is at most 1 h old, spreads are 1c at the median, prices are in dollars (never above 1), and the code path is the same one holdout2 used. 10 of the 46 fresh events had nothing qualifying, either because every word was already at 1c/99c when the rule looked (the speech ended more than 3 h before Kalshi closed) or because there were no candles before the look time. idea.name: Polymarket US BTC mid-window stale quotes vs our index fair (incl. macro-release seconds)
idea.family: cross-venue: Polymarket US + our CF feed
idea.mechanism: Compute P(settle >= strike) every second from the CF index (pinrun maths with longer time to expiry) and buy Up at the ask or Down at (1 - bid) when price clears fair by the 0.0695*p*(1-p) taker fee plus a margin; in particular in the first seconds after 8:30 ET / 2:00 PM ET releases, when BTC moves 0.3-1% and small Poly makers may be slow to pull.
idea.why_mispriced: Hypothesis: slow retail/makers on low-volume Poly books do not reprice as fast as BTC moves (the book showed the same levels for many seconds while the index moved).
idea.must_be_true: The fair model is calibrated (it is crude: sigma from trailing 30 min, no drift, no fat tails; disagreeing with the market for hundreds of seconds is exactly what a mis-set sigma produces); Poly resting orders survive >= 1 s after a jump in size worth the fee. Measured: Poly lags Kalshi by a median 1.85 s and the lag is mostly gone within 1 s after jumps (3 of 69 jumps gave >= 5c at +1 s).
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: Unknown, weak: < $1-2/day at a $60 balance even if real.
idea.data_needed: Run sweep/crypto-other/poly1h.py on ~72 hourly windows of the 3-day recording and calibrate: for every second flagged 'edge > 5c', did the flagged side win more than its price + fee (clustered by window, >= 30 flagged windows); keep the recorder running through Oct 1-2 12:30Z releases.
idea.evidence_so_far: 4 recorded 1h windows (03Z-06Z 09-25): seconds with model edge > 5c after fee: 03Z 16 up / 2 down; 04Z 27 / 89; 05Z 14 / 9; 06Z (partial) hundreds both ways (noisy). Outcomes UP, DOWN, DOWN; n=3 is nothing. No release recorded on the Poly book yet. lag_hedge.py results as in I44.

chk.measured:
Answer first: the 1-hour part is dead, the release-seconds part is untested, and the 15-minute part only shows an edge if we act within about 1 second of an index print. By 2-3 seconds it is noise.

Everything below is a replay of Polymarket's own recorded prices against the BRTI tape. Per the operator's rule, that makes it a hypothesis, not evidence. Folder: C:/Users/Joe/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--kals-repo/47b37ac1-655c-4d72-a81b-a48e9625d5bd/scratchpad/sweep/check-I53/

1) THE FAIR MODEL, CHECKED ON THE INDEX ALONE (calib.py -> calib3.out, calib_out.json). Used 30 days of BRTI: 672 one-hour windows and 2,742 fifteen-minute windows, checked at fixed times to close and clustered by window.
- Overall it is calibrated to within about 2-5c.
- It is overconfident when volatility is rising (5-min vol / 30-min vol >= 1.25): the favourite wins 3-10c less often than it says.
- In the last 7 days it was overconfident by 2-8c in the 0.70-0.99 buckets.
- In 15m windows it is overconfident by 2-4c whenever it says 0.90-0.99.
- Strike convention checked: the mean of the 60 prints BEFORE the boundary matches Kalshi's official KXBTC15M strike to within 0.005 on 46 of 46 windows. The other convention is off by a median of 0.27.

2) EVERY POLYMARKET WINDOW SINCE LAUNCH, OUT OF SAMPLE (ph_fetch.py -> ph_all.json; histpoly.py -> hps_d0..3.out).
- Data: 53 one-hour and 211 fifteen-minute windows from 09-22 15Z to 09-25 14Z.
- Price source: public /v1/price-history. Its longPrice is the cost to buy Up and shortPrice is the cost to buy Down. Checked against my recorded live book (ph_cmp.py, verify.out): median difference 0c, 90th percentile +1c. So this is not the 30-second-cache problem that faked an arbitrage before.
- Fair value: the model's reading passed through a calibration table built only from windows that ended BEFORE launch, split by volatility regime.

ref.strongest_objection:
Nothing here is a slow Polymarket quote we could beat to. The one profitable slice, favourites at the second of the index print, has three problems. First, the checker picked it after seeing the results. Second, it lines up with a 3-day stretch in which favourites beat underdogs on both venues. Third, it vanishes on a sample six times bigger.

(1) The idea as written trades both sides whenever price clears fair value plus the fee. Using my own model, frozen before the test, on the same 211 Polymarket 15-minute windows (09-22 15Z to 09-25 14Z), that rule nets about +2c per window if we act at the print. It nets -2c, -3c and -4c per window if we act 1, 2 or 3 seconds late. Underdog buys lose at every delay: -8.8c per window at 0 s (t -2.3). The checker's own run also has underdogs losing at every delay.

(2) Slow quotes would help both sides and would fade within about a second. What I found does neither. On the same windows, Polymarket beat Kalshi on favourites by about 7c per window at every delay (7.5 / 5.8 / 7.7 / 8.1c at 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 s), and Polymarket did worse than Kalshi on underdogs. Separately, I checked a fixed schedule of moments (not ones our model picked): buying the favourite on Polymarket cost 5.3c per window more than on Kalshi (t -2.3), and underdogs cost 27.7c per window more (t -5.3). There is no cheap level on Polymarket to buy.

(3) The checker's statement that "the whole market lags the print by about 1 second" rests on Kalshi's ticker feed. That feed sends about one message per second per market: gaps between messages are 0.98-1.02 s for the middle half, on four hours checked across 09-12 to 09-25. A once-a-second feed cannot measure a lag of under a second. My own attempt at a sub-second fill test on that feed produced a fake +4c per window, because it priced fills at the ticker snapshot from before the print.

(4) A larger sample kills it. I ran the same frozen model and rule over 1,227 Kalshi windows (09-09 to 09-22), buying favourites at the price shown when the index printed. Result: -0.7c per window (se 2.1c, t -0.4). Day by day it swung between about -$17 and +$11 per contract. The checker's +12.8c per window is about 6 standard errors from that.

(5) On the live Polymarket book, timed to the millisecond (today, 21 windows), the flagged ask moved up only 0.3-0.4c on average in the first 0.15-0.5 s. So the flags are mostly the model disagreeing with the market, not quotes waiting to be picked off.

Operational problems, each of which also caps it:
- Polymarket paid our one real bet about 82 minutes after the close, so money is locked up for about 97 minutes per trade.
- $50 of the $60.52 balance is a held promotional bonus.
- Some 15-minute windows do not exist at all: 11:00-11:45Z today returned 404.
- The order tool (polyorder.py) allows 5 contracts per order, one order per window, $10 at risk and $5 of losses per day, and needs a one-time approval code for every order.
- It is the same Bitcoin move the live Kalshi bot is already exposed to.

idea.name: Blowout pin: MLB leader entering the 9th up 6 or more
idea.family: sports / late-game near-certain (pinrun analogue)
idea.mechanism: Build a win-probability table from statsapi linescores (7,246 regular-season games 2024-2026, free). When a 9th half-inning starts with the leader up 6+, bid 99c on the leader; hold 10-20 minutes to settlement. Football version needs its own table (ESPN linescores 2019-2025).
idea.why_mispriced: Price is capped at 99c by the 1c tick; once the outcome is >= 99.86% the cap leaves up to ~0.9c; sellers are winners cashing out.
idea.must_be_true: The table's loss rate holds (2 losses in 2,273 half-inning starts with lead 6+, 0.09%; 95% upper bound per cell 0.45-0.51%) AND we get filled at 99c -- the tape says there is essentially NO offer to lift: in 14 games with the leader up 4+ entering the 9th, takers bought the leader at <= 98c only 58 contracts in total, and at 99c zero in 10 of 14 games. At 4 runs in the top 9th (loss 0.77%, upper bound 1.67%) 98c prints happened (CIN-ATL 100k, STL-PIT 51k) but the upper bound makes 98c negative.
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: $0-10/day (weak): ~+0.5-0.9c/contract after fees at 99c on ~3 qualifying MLB games a day, only until the season ends 09-27 (postseason 1-4 games/day).
idea.data_needed: The same 1/s book polling as I26 from the top of the 9th; a football table if pursued.
idea.evidence_so_far: Table (w1.out): 9th top, lead 6+: 1,427 starts, 0.14% lost; 9th bottom, lead 6+: 846 starts, 0 lost; top 9th lead 5: 0.46%; lead 4: 0.77%. Kalshi's leader price at 56 late half-inning starts in 40 games averaged 1.1c BELOW the table; the only positive cells are at the 99c cap (9th, lead 6+ priced 0.989-0.990 vs table 0.999-1.000, +1.0c). NFL LV-LAC 09-20: LAC up 10 with 2:29 left, ESPN WP 99.9%, Kalshi at 99c immediately. Files in sweep/sports-games/.

idea.novelty_vs_killed: Loss rate from the raw score feed (pincalib spirit), not a tape loss rate; new market family for pinrun's logic.

chk.measured:
WHY IT DIES: in games that are really decided, nobody offers the leader below 99c, so there is nothing for us to buy. The only way in is to rest a bid at 99c and wait in line behind everyone else bidding 99c. That bid pays +1c when the leader wins and -99c when they lose, and it mostly gets filled in the games where the leader then loses.

1) TICK AND FEES, read from the API today (a1_api.py, a1_api.json). KXMLBGAME, KXNFLGAME and KXNCAAFGAME all move in whole cents from 0 to $1, so 99c is the highest bid anyone can post. Fee type is quadratic_with_maker_fees, so resting orders pay a fee too; the multiplier is 0.5 for MLB and 1 for NFL and NCAAF. Fees are billed to the hundredth of a cent, so at 99c the fee is negligible and is not what kills this. Settlement rules add no real risk here. An MLB game that is delayed stays open for up to 2 days. An NFL tie pays 50c, which cannot happen from a 17-point lead.

2) FOOTBALL SUPPLY, new pull (b1_fb_supply.py -> b1_fb.json, tallied by b2_fb_an.py -> b2.out). 68 Kalshi games: NFL week 3 plus NCAAF on 09-19, matched to ESPN play-by-play. 116 Kalshi GETs. The leader is decided from the score only, never from the final result. From the moment the state was reached (plus 30 s for our feed to catch up) until the final whistle, I counted what takers bought from the leader's resting offers:
- Leader up 17+ with 5:00 or less left: 39 games (6 NFL, 33 NCAAF). Leader bought at 98c or less: 0 contracts. At 99c: 0.
- Leader up 21+ with 8:00 or less left: 34 games. 0 and 0.
- Leader up 24+ at any point in Q4: 32 games. 0 and 0.
- Re-run assuming our feed has no delay at all (b2z.out): still 0 contracts at 98c or less in every decided cell.
- The one cell that did offer cheap leader contracts is the one where the leader LOST. KXNCAAFGAME-26SEP19TEMTOL: Temple led 42-28 with 2:00 left, Toledo tied it at 0:54 and won 49-48 in overtime. Checked against ESPN's scoring plays (b3_temtol.py). Kalshi held Temple at 99c for about 7 minutes after the state was reached, then the whole line of 99c bids got filled on the way down to 96c within one minute. Takers then bought 554,309 Temple contracts at 96c or less. Cheap supply showed up only in the game that went wrong.

3) FLOW INTO THE 99c LINE IN GAMES THE LEADER WON. This is contracts sold at 99c, the only thing that could ever fill our bid.
- NCAAF, leader up 17+ with 5:00 left: median 100 contracts per game across 33 games (only 9 games reached 900).
- NFL, same state: median 15,879 per game across 6 games.
- MLB, leader up 6+ at the start of a 9th-inning half (earlier file sports-games/w3.out): median 5,517 per game across 10 games. Buyers taking the leader at 98c or less in those games: 0 contracts. In 9 of the 10, the 99c line was never emptied.
- How long the line is has NOT been measured for these sports. The only comparison is other near-decided sports markets on 09-24 (sports-games/q1_queue.jsonl: women's ITF tennis and test cricket), which had 120,000 to 195,000 contracts already waiting at 99c. That is far more than the MLB or NFL flow above, and NCAAF blowouts against weak teams sit at 99c from before kickoff.

4) THE BREAK-EVEN. Per game, with B contracts bid at 99c, a loss rate L, and q = the share of our bid filled in games the leader wins: EV = q x B x 1c - L x B x 99c, because in a losing game the whole line gets filled. So we need q above roughly 100 x L.
- MLB: L = 0.09% (2 losses in 2,273 9th-inning starts with a lead of 6+, from the raw MLB score feed; 95% upper bound about 0.3%). We need at least 9% of our bid filled in wins (30% at the upper bound).
- NFL and NCAAF: L is unmeasured, since no historical football table was built. This sample alone: 0 of 39 losses at 17+ with 5:00 left, 1 of 40 at 14+ with 2:00 left.
- NCAAF fails even at the FRONT of the line. Filling our 900 against the actual flow gives $121 gross over 33 games, $3.67 per game. At L = 0.5% the losses cost $4.46 per game, so it is negative. It is only positive if L is under about 0.4%, and the front of the line is not on offer anyway.

REALISTIC, $900 bank: about $0/day, and likely slightly negative. Buying: $0, because 0 contracts were offered in the 49 decided games checked. Resting a 99c bid: if the line ahead of us is as long as the 100,000-200,000 seen in similar markets, almost none of our bid fills in games the leader wins. Every game we sit in then costs L x $891 in expectation, about -$0.80 to -$1.80 per game at L = 0.09-0.2%.

CEILING, only if we were somehow FIRST in the 99c line every game, which we would not be:
- MLB: 900 x 1c x 0.999 - 0.0009 x $891 = about +$8.2 per game. About 3 games a day, but only through 09-27, then about 8 qualifying playoff games in all of October. About $110 in total, then nothing until the 2027 season.
- NFL: about +$7-8 per game (the loss rate is assumed, not measured) x 5-6 games a week = about $6/day.
- NCAAF: $3.67 per game gross minus $1.78-4.46 in losses = -$0.8 to +$1.9 per game.
- The capital is also tied up for 10-40 minutes and NFL games all end at the same time, so at $900 we would get one game per time slot at most.

$5k bank: WORSE per dollar. What we can win is capped by how much gets sold at 99c (median 5,517 contracts per game in MLB, 15,879 in NFL, 100 in NCAAF, before anyone ahead of us in line takes their share). What we lose in a comeback grows with our full bid: a 5,000-contract bid loses $4,950. First in line, NFL tops out at about $50 per game, which is about $40/day. Behind the queue, still about $0.
chk.worst_case: One comeback while our whole bid sits at 99c: -$891 at the $900 bank, or -$4,950 with a 5,000-contract bid at $5k. That wipes out about 110 of the best-possible +$8 games. It really happens: KXNCAAFGAME-26SEP19TEMTOL (leader up 14 with 2:00 left, lost in overtime) filled the entire 99c line within one minute. Across one season of about 100 qualifying NFL games at an assumed 0.1-0.2% loss rate, the chance of at least one such loss is about 10-20%.
chk.killer_risks: (1) No one sells below the cap: 0 contracts at 98c or less in 39 of 39 football games at 17+ with 5:00 left and in 10 of 10 MLB games with a 6+ lead in the 9th. (2) The fills we would get are the bad ones. In winning games the flow almost never reaches the back of the 99c line (in 9 of 10 MLB lead-6+ games the line was never emptied), while in a losing game the whole line fills (TEM-TOL). So the loss rate on OUR fills is far above the table's 0.09-0.2%, and break-even needs 9-20%+ of our bid filled in wins. (3) The line starts long before we would join: cupcake NCAAF games sit at 99c from before kickoff, and similar sports markets had 120,000-195,000 contracts waiting at 99c. (4) Calendar: MLB's regular season ends 09-27; the playoffs give about 8 qualifying games in October. (5) Football loss rates are unmeasured: no historical table was built, and the one-week sample already has a 14-point, 2:00-left loss. (6) A bigger bank makes it worse, because the gain is capped by the 99c flow while the loss grows with bid size.

chk.measured:
Why it's dead: the free MLB feed deliberately runs late. It showed a pitch a median 9.2 s after it happened. The stale Kalshi offers on home-run rungs are bought 0.7-0.9 s after the pitch, and on strikeout rungs a median 3-4.7 s after. The free feed can also show a strikeout that is later taken back, which makes a bot buy the wrong rung.

1) The archive made it look alive, and that was a bug. The archive of past feed snapshots (/feed/live/timestamps) shows each strike three or home run in a snapshot stamped the same second as the pitch (139/139 strikeout locks and 50/50 home-run locks, 09-22..24). Read that way, arriving 1 s after the pitch would have been worth up to $772/day at $900 and $1,363/day at $5k (3 days, 294 locks, capsim3.out). I checked whether the stamp means 'published'. It does not.

2) Live test today, Cubs at Red Sox game 1 (from about 1:08 PM ET). I polled the feed 3 times a second with the cache bypassed (every reply came fresh from MLB's server); my clock was within 0.02 s of true time. Over 105 pitches, the feed showed each pitch a median 9.2 s after the pitch time (10th percentile 3.6 s, 90th 16.2 s, worst 39 s). A normal, cached poll saw it a median 15.6 s late. MLB's push channel marks its messages "isDelay": true and was no faster. Four free endpoints (full feed, trimmed feed, play-by-play, line score) updated together, so there is no faster free source. File: live_824703.jsonl, endpoints_824703.jsonl.

3) The fast buyers are ahead of any free-feed user.
- Home runs: almost every one (solo and with runners on) gets its cheap ladder of 1-10 contract offers bought 0.71-0.96 s after the pitch time. Someone has a faster feed.
- Strikeouts: the first buy at 98c or more comes a median 3.0 / 4.7 / 3.9 s after (09-22 / 23 / 24). On 09-22, 15 of 108 locks were bought at about 1 s.

Using the 105 live delays against 3 days of tape, the most we could have reached is $79/day (strikeouts) plus $104/day (solo home runs), before fees. That assumes we beat every other buyer after the feed arrives. But every free-feed bot gets the same late update at the same moment. It is a race decided in milliseconds, and we sit 80-110 ms from Kalshi.

4) False signals: the archive hides them. At 1:21:05 PM ET the live feed showed a called strike three, including a finished 'strikeout', for Clay Holmes. At 1:21:22 it changed to a ball (the batter challenged and won). The archive now shows that pitch as a ball from the start. So my archive replay, 0 false out of 480 strike-three signals over 09-23/24 (falsesig_*.out), is itself wrong. Live, 1 of the first ~5 strike-three signals was reversed. Separately, the final records show 7 overturned strike threes in 3 days (abs.out).

5) My read-only paper bot, which pulls the Kalshi book the moment it detects a lock (snap_824703.jsonl):
- Holmes 2+ strikeouts: 14 s after the pitch, only 17 contracts at 97c were left, worth $0.51. No trades hit that rung; the market maker had pulled its offers.
- The reversal above threw its count off by one. On his real 2nd strikeout it would have bought the 3+ rung, which was NOT decided (YES bids 56-59c, sellers at 58-59c afterwards). That book had 730 contracts offered at 89-97c.

6) Home runs: bases empty plus 'In play, run(s)' was a home run 74 of 74 times over 5 days of final records (hrclass.out). That is useless when the feed is 9 s late and someone buys at 0.8 s.

About 700 Kalshi GETs in total. The collector, crypto feeds and live bot were all running when checked; 86.8 GB disk free.
chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
About $0/day at either bank size.

- Ceiling at $900, on a full regular-season day of 12-16 games: $79 + $104 = $183/day before fees. That only holds if we won every race after the feed arrived, and against bots getting the same late update from 80-110 ms away we would lose most of them.
- Only 2 such days remain (09-26 and 09-27, 14 games each). Then the playoffs run about 4 games/day, falling to 1/day, through about Oct 31. After that there are no games until late March 2027.
- The one correctly matched live lock left $0.51.
- $5k does not help, because money is not the limit; the available cheap offers are. Nothing is cheap left by the time the free feed arrives.
chk.worst_case: Seen live today. The feed showed a called strike three, then took it back 17 s later when the batter challenged and won. A bot counting strikeouts from the free feed then buys the next rung up, which is not decided. The 3+ rung had 730 contracts offered at 89-97c while it was really worth about 58-59c. That is about -$250 on one event at full size; at the $900 bank the bet would be ~$650 and the loss ~$230-250. A counting or name-matching bug repeated across a night of games could lose several hundred dollars in one day.
chk.killer_risks:
- MLB's free feed is deliberately late: a median 9.2 s behind the pitch, 90th percentile 16 s, flagged "isDelay": true. Every free endpoint and the push channel run at the same delay.
- Home-run offers are bought 0.7-0.9 s after the pitch and strikeout offers a median 3-4.7 s after, by buyers with faster data.
- The free feed publishes strike threes that are later taken back, and the archive rewrites them, so replays understate how often a signal is wrong.
- Every other free-feed bot sees the same update at the same moment, so it is a millisecond race from a home laptop.
- About 2 regular-season days are left, then the playoffs, then nothing until April.
- MLB's data terms allow only "individual, non-commercial, non-bulk use" (gdx.mlb.com/components/copyright.txt), so trading on it arguably breaks their terms.
chk.next_test:
None on free data; it's killed. It could only come back with an official paid feed that isn't delayed (Sportradar or Genius; price not checked; expect enterprise pricing).
- Cheapest decisive step: ask the vendor for its pitch-to-publish delay and its price. It passes only if the delay is under 0.5 s and the price is under 10% of the $180/day ceiling.
- Even then, the 0.7-0.9 s home-run buyer shows someone already has that data.
- A paid feed would still need a live check of reversals: log every strike three that is taken back and wait out the challenge before buying on a called strike three.
chk.capital_needed: None worth committing. Money is not what limits this; the free data is too late.

idea.name: Replay-review window pricing
idea.family: sports / rules x official feed
idea.mechanism: When a game-ending play is challenged (statsapi reviewDetails, ESPN plays), price the overturn chance from historical overturn rates by play type times the win probability if the game continues; take whichever side the market misprices during the ~60 s review.
idea.why_mispriced: Traders anchor on the call on the field (MIA-AZ 09-16: winner traded 95-98c for ~60 s during a challenge; if ~45% of such challenges were overturned and AZ then had ~22%, fair would be ~90c).
idea.must_be_true: Overturn rates for game-ending plays are much higher than the ~3% the market priced; TV replays (seen by bettors before any feed) may already settle it.
idea.rough_dollars_per_day: $0-2/day (perhaps 30-60 such reviews a season).
idea.data_needed: statsapi reviewDetails across 7,246 games (free): overturn rate for challenged final plays, plus Kalshi trades inside each review window.
idea.evidence_so_far: One case: KXMLBGAME-26SEP162140MIAAZ, challenged by team 109, not overturned; winner back to 99c at ~+60 s.

chk.measured:
WHY IT'S DEAD: the idea assumed about 45 of 100 challenged game-ending calls get overturned. The real number is 7 of 100 (non-robot reviews). Even when a call was overturned, the team that got the reprieve went on to win 0 times out of 21. The long shot won 0 of 107 game-ending reviews on Kalshi's tape, and during those reviews it cost about 2c. Buying it lost the whole stake every time.

What I measured and how:
1) MLB official play-by-play (statsapi), every completed 2025 and 2026 game, 4,862 games. 3,538 reviews in the 8th inning or later. Script: pull_mlb.py.
 - Non-robot reviews (manager challenge or umpire review) of a call that ENDED the game: 54 (50 upheld, 4 overturned = 7%). Managers throw their last challenge at hopeless plays.
 - 2026 robot-umpire (ABS) challenges on a pitch where a strike ends the game (2 outs, 2 strikes, fielding team ahead), 124 in total. Script: pull_abs.py.
   (a) The strike was called on the field, so the game was over, and the batter challenged: 55 (37 upheld, 18 overturned = 33%). The batting team still won 0 of 55, and 0 of the 18 overturns.
   (b) Ball called with 2 strikes and the fielding team challenged: 68 (18 overturned). The fielding team won 65 of 68 anyway.
2) Kalshi KXMLBGAME trades around every one of those calls, 40s before to 150s after, in time buckets. Scripts: kreview.py, kabs.py, anal.py, fav.py, fav2.py. I checked every market's result against the MLB winner and 1 of 68 was the wrong doubleheader game, so I dropped it.
 - Non-robot, 52 matched events: the long shot's average ask was 2.2 to 2.5c from 15 to 60s after the call. It won 0 of 52, a loss of 2.3c per contract per event. The long shot was OVER-priced, not under-priced. In the MIA-AZ example (Sep 17, about 12:31 AM ET), AZ traded at 2-5c during the review, while 7% overturn x about 20% chance AZ comes back after an overturn = about 1.5c fair.
 - Robot challenges, 55 events: the long-shot ask was about 2.3c and it won 0 of 55. Knowing the overturn in advance would not have helped: after an overturn the batting team won 0 of 18, and the market barely moved on overturns (2.1c vs 2.4c).
 - Reverse side (buy the favorite during the review): 107 wins, 0 losses, at a median price of 98.3 to 98.4c. But 0 losses in 107 still allows a true loss rate up to about 3 in 100, and the break-even at 98.4c is 1.6 in 100. Estimated loss rate: robot challenges 33% overturned x about 7% comeback = about 2.3 in 100, which loses money. Non-robot 6% x about 15% = about 1 in 100, worth maybe +0.7c a contract, unproven.
3) NFL (ESPN play-by-play, 319 games: 2025 regular season and playoffs plus 2026 weeks 1-3, script pull_nfl.py): 34 reviews in the last 2 minutes of the 4th quarter or overtime. Only 7 had the game riding on it (score within 8, at most 3 plays left), 3 of them reversed. That is about 6 a season, too few to matter, so I did not pull the Kalshi tape for them.

Checks on anything that looked good:
 - The class 'final play reviewed AND overturned' showed the helped team winning 15 of 15 at +4 to +9c. That is fake: it only includes overturns that ended the game, so it is chosen by the result. Discarded.
 - One robot-challenge event was misclassified (the market was at 33c and the game went on). Removed.
 - Kalshi trades older than 2026-07-27 only come back from /historical/trades. My first pass returned nothing for them and was redone.
Kalshi calls used: about 450 GETs. Both collectors were alive at the end (crypto_feeds pid 105352, 24 MB; kalshi_collector pid 2532788, 43 MB). 85.4 GB disk free.

chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
The idea as proposed (buy the long shot during the review) loses money. It lost the whole stake 107 of 107 times, about -2.3c a contract per event. There are about 0.3 events a day in season (107 over about 350 baseball days; about 0.5 a day in 2026 because of robot challenges).
At the $900 bank: 300 contracts x 2.3c = about -$7 an event x 0.3 a day = about -$2 a day.
At a $5k bank: about -$10 a day.
The reverse side (non-robot reviews only, buying the favorite at about 98.3c): about 27 events a season, 0.15 a day.
At $900: 300 contracts, $295 at risk, x +0.7c = +$2.10 an event, about +$0.30 a day. One comeback costs about -$295.
At $5k: 1,500 contracts x 0.7c = $10.50 an event, about +$1.60 a day. One comeback costs about -$1,475.
That +0.7c is an estimate, not a measurement. Supply for us was not measured either: the 3,000 to 30,000 long-shot contracts that traded in these windows were other people's flow, not proof we would get filled. The operator should read it as roughly $0 a day.
chk.worst_case: Long-shot side: lose the whole stake on every event, as measured (0 of 107 paid). Favorite side: a call gets overturned and the trailing team comes back, so we lose about 98c per contract. At 300 contracts that is about -$295, a third of the $900 bank, on one event. The chance is roughly 1 to 3 events in 100 per review, and higher for robot challenges.
chk.killer_risks:
1) The premise is wrong: game-ending calls are overturned 7 times in 100 for non-robot reviews (4 of 54), not about 45. Robot challenges are overturned 33 times in 100, but the team that benefits still almost never wins (0 of 18).
2) The market already prices the long shot at or above fair (about 2c during the review).
3) The reverse bet is the same shape as pinrun (tiny wins, rare 98c losses), with 0.15 to 0.5 events a day. The sample cannot show the loss rate is below break-even.
4) TV viewers see replay angles before any data feed shows a review in progress. Any fill we get on the favorite is likely from someone who has seen the replay (adverse selection).
5) NFL has about 6 qualifying reviews a season.
6) Kalshi charges makers too on KXMLBGAME (0.5x multiplier), and statsapi does not give a review start/end time, so the review window can only be inferred from the tape.
chk.next_test: None is worth running for this idea. The data that decides it (107 Kalshi events with overturn outcomes) says no. If the favorite side (non-robot game-ending reviews) is ever worth a look, the cheapest test is a paper logger for the rest of the 2026 postseason and 2027. It would poll the statsapi live feed for reviewDetails.inProgress=true on a game-ending call and record the Kalshi favorite ask at detection +5s and +15s. Pass bar, written before looking: at least 60 events with a mean favorite ask at detection of 98.0c or lower AND a mean overturn-then-comeback rate of 1 in 100 or less. It would take about 2 seasons to reach, so it is not worth doing.
chk.capital_needed: None: not recommended. The favorite side would put about $300 at risk per event at the $900 bank, for about $2 expected per event.

chk.measured:
The earlier "dead" call was based on a misread of the tape. Tennis walkovers are not dead because the market is efficient: they are dead for us because one very fast outside trader takes almost all of the money within a fraction of a second.

What the tape shows (Kalshi trade history, read-only, 21 days to 2026-09-25, 6 tennis series, 9,060 settled markets in 4,530 matches):
- 32 matches were voided and paid both players 50c: 14 marked 'Match WOV' (walkover) and 18 marked 'Competitor mismatch' (Kalshi listed a pairing that never played). That is about 1.5 a day, almost all of them ITF events. There were also 37 other 'fair price' settlements (for example 0.21/0.79), but their trades were small (-$809 in total).
- Earlier this was read as the book repricing within the same second. It is actually a taker buying up the whole stale book in one instant, in both player markets inside the same 10 ms. Examples: TANHUX at 03:45:38.22Z bought 19,800 HU YES at 4-14c, 7,594 more at 14-48c and 18,128 TANG NO at 4-36c, worth about $16.3k. WILGER at 08:23:39.36Z bought 4,803 GER YES at 7-45c and 2,628 WIL NO, worth about $1.6k.
- Taker profit in those sweeps, valued at the 50c payout minus the 0.07·p·(1-p) fee: $86,015 across the 64 voided markets in 21 days, about $4,100 a day. Per match the median was $1,293, the top was $16,315, and 20 of 32 matches paid at least $500. Median sweep size was 10,234 contracts. In 22 of 23 matches the sweep lasted 0.00-0.12 s. The one exception, a '157 s' reading on TANHUX, was an error in my own detector: it chained in ordinary trades at 4c from before the sweep.
- Anyone arriving second got nothing. After the sweep instant, not one trade happened more than 6c from 50c in any match. Taker trades after the sweep worth at least 1c net totalled $9.75 over 21 days, about $0.46 a day.
- There was no sign the news leaked early. In the 30 minutes before each sweep, the 37,238 contracts traded at stale prices lost $4,408 in total for the takers, meaning they were on the wrong side.
- Resting buy orders after the sweep: every trade below 50c afterwards is a sure gain for whoever buys the cheap side. Resting orders collected $5,010 on 192,770 contracts over 28 matches, about 2.6c a contract, or about $239 a day for all bidders together. That is lopsided: WILGER alone was $3,044, where someone kept dumping 18k-contract blocks at 46-49c. Without it the total is about $94 a day. Median time from sweep to market close was 3.2 h, so money is tied up for only a few hours.
- Public sources a bot can read: the ITF site/API returns an anti-bot challenge page, not data, and Sofascore's API returns 403. Flashscore's HTML loads (757 KB). The official ITF app is built by Sportradar, so the sweeper most likely runs on Sportradar's paid feed for businesses, which has no public price.
- Check for a fake result: by hand, TANHUX adds up to roughly $15k against $16.3k measured. Prices are in dollars and counts are contracts. Only matches that ended at 50c were studied, which is right for measuring how big the prize is, but it means false alarms (a sweep toward 50c on a match that was then played) were NOT measured.
- MLB called games: not re-measured. The earlier base rate (11 'Completed Early' games out of 7,246 finals, 0.15%) stands. On top of that, the regular season ends within days and playoff games are suspended and finished later, never called early, so this cannot happen at all until about late March 2027.
- Both recorders were alive after the jobs (pids 105352 at 24 MB and 2532788 at 43 MB). Free disk was 85.5 GB.

chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
Arriving first (take the stale book): $0 a day realistically. The prize is real, about $4,100 a day, but a feed-driven bot takes it within 10 ms every time, and every public source we can script is blocked or slower. Arriving second as a taker: measured $9.75 in 21 days, about $0.46 a day, at any bank size.

Resting orders after the sweep: none of this is measured, it is an upper limit. The idea is to post both-sided bids at 49c, which earns 1c a contract, since sellers were filling at 46-48c. If we got every contract of the observed flow, that is 192,770 contracts × 1c ÷ 21 days = about $92 a day, but only with unlimited money (WILGER alone would need about $47k).
- At a $900 bank we can hold about 1,800 contracts per match at 49c. About 10 of the 28 matches had meaningful flow, so 10 × 1,800 × 1c ÷ 21 days = about $9 a day at best. If we only win part of the queue, more like $1-4 a day.
- At $5k we can hold about 10,000 contracts per match, so roughly $40-50 a day at best and $5-25 a day realistically. The flow itself caps it near $92 a day.
- Fees: none. Resting orders pay no fee on the ITF series (fee_type 'quadratic', not 'quadratic_with_maker_fees'), and the lopsided WILGER-type flow may not come back.
chk.worst_case:
The worst case is a false void signal while holding one side. We bid 49c on an underdog because a sweep or report said walkover, but the match is actually played and the underdog loses. At the $900 size that is 1,800 × $0.49 = about -$882, the whole bank, on one match. At $5k it is about -$4,900.

Bidding both sides of the same market caps this. A filled pair costs 98c and always pays $1, whether or not the match is voided. So the real risk is only the unbalanced part of the position, which should be capped at around $50.

The false-alarm rate is UNMEASURED. For the first-arriver route, the worst case is the same: acting on a public report that turns out to be wrong.
chk.killer_risks:
1. Speed against a professional. The whole $4,100 a day goes to one actor who buys both markets within 10 ms, very likely on the official Sportradar feed (the official ITF app is built by Sportradar). ITF's public site blocks bots and Sofascore returns 403. Scraping Flashscore at 30-60 s intervals would lose every race we observed.
2. The after-sweep flow depends on one lopsided seller. 61% of it ($3,044 of $5,010) came from one match where someone kept dumping 18k-contract blocks. Every other bidder competes for the same 49c spot, and the sweeper can post bids there too.
3. False alarms were not measured. I only looked at matches that ended at 50c. A both-sided position removes most of this risk; a one-sided one keeps it.
4. 'Competitor mismatch' is Kalshi's own ruling after the fact. It paid 50c in all 18 cases here, but it is Kalshi's decision, not a rule a bot can check ahead of time.
5. Small sample: 21 days, 32 voided matches, of which 23 had real sweeps and about 10 had after-sweep flow worth anything. One lopsided match could be rare, and the pattern could stop if the market makers who get swept start pulling their orders faster.
6. MLB part: dead. The base rate is 0.15%, and nothing can happen until about late March 2027 because playoff games are suspended, not called.
chk.next_test:
Build a paper watcher only: no orders, all GET/WebSocket reads. Run it about 14 days, which should catch about 20 voided matches at the 1.5 a day seen here. For every open ITF and Challenger match market it would:
(a) watch the Kalshi ticker or trade feed and log each sweep instant, meaning a jump to about 50c in both player markets within 1 s;
(b) check Flashscore, the one public source a script can read, every 30 s for each listed match and log the first moment it shows a walkover, a withdrawal or a different opponent;
(c) for 30 minutes after each sweep, record the book and simulate our both-sided 49c bids placed last in the queue, filling only on trades priced at 49c or worse.

Pass bars, written before any data is seen:
- Arriving first: Flashscore shows the void at least 5 s before the Kalshi sweep in 5 or more of the first 15 voided matches, and at our moment of knowing, at least $50 of stale depth was still on the book. If not, the first-arriver route is dead for good.
- Resting orders after the sweep: at least $5 a day of simulated fills at the $900 cap, with no single match giving more than half of it, and zero voided matches that failed to settle at 50c.

Cost: about 1 day to build, one extra WebSocket connection on the rate limit, and $0 of data. Before building, it would be worth pricing Sportradar's ITF feed. If it costs more than a few hundred dollars a month, the first-arriver route cannot pay at this bank size, even though the prize is $4k a day.
chk.capital_needed: Resting orders after the sweep: about $900 per match at the $900 cap, tied up for a median of 3.2 h (sweep to close, then settlement about 2 min later). Up to about $5k at the larger bank; the flow itself would use up to about $47k in a lopsided match. Arriving first: the median sweep was about 10k contracts at 4-40c, around $1-4k per match. Being first would also most likely need a paid official data feed, which has no public price.

ref.strongest_objection:
The checker's plan to rest 49c bids after a sweep relied on "bid both sides so a filled pair always pays $1, and the leftover risk is capped near $50". That breaks, because the money after a sweep flows one way only. Nearly everyone selling into the 46-49c bids is dumping the same side: the longshot holders cashing out, and in WILGER a stale market maker that sold GER YES in blocks of 7-17k contracts every few seconds (all "GER no" in the tape). So the two sides almost never pair up.

With one-sided exposure capped at 100 contracts (the checker's ~$50 limit), the whole 21-day gain from voided matches falls from $99.73 to $10.09, about $0.48 a day. Without the cap, the bot holds one side at 49c, and every time its "sweep" detector fires on a match that is then played, it loses almost the full position.

Measured on a random 220 of the 2,966 ITF matches that settled normally in the same 21 days:
- The checker's own trigger (both player markets jump to about 50c within 1 s) fired in 21 of 220 played matches, versus 11 of 35 real voids. Simulated fills lost $2,937 in the sample, as much as $882 in a single match at the $900 cap, which scales to about -$1,900 a day.
- The strictest trigger that still catches voids (both prices at least 25c from 50 beforehand, then held inside 44-56c for 120 s) had 0 false fires in 220. Its best case is $3.35 a day at $900, and it assumes we are alone at the best bid and get every contract sold at 49c or lower.
- 0 of 220 cannot rule out a false-fire rate of up to about 3 in 220 matches, roughly 40 over 21 days. At about -$600 to -$880 per false fire, break-even needs fewer than about 1 false fire per 25,000 matches. A 14-day paper watcher (about 2,000 matches) cannot show that.
- A $5k bank adds nothing: capacity barely binds, $70.25 at a 1,800-contract cap versus $70.25 at 10,000.

Competition is also already there. In SAWOHA, 4,688 of the 5,412 resting fills were at 49c, so someone was already bidding there. In the three unlabeled 50c voids, 183k of 212k contracts filled at 49c. The sweeper, who knows first, can post 49c bids in the same instant.

The first-arriver route stays dead (the checker agrees: a feed-driven sweep completes in about 10 ms). The MLB part is dead until spring 2027.

chk.measured:
The idea's premise is wrong in one way and the idea fails for a different reason. These books are not thin. They are fast, and a free score feed arrives after the price has already moved.

1) VOLUME. Kalshi GET /markets and /markets/trades, last 14 days, 106+ trade-history GETs in total. Contracts traded while the game was being played, per game: La Liga 2 33k-178k (9 games), 2. Bundesliga 54k-174k (7), 3. Liga 7k-58k (29), KBO 24k-246k (7), NPB 44k-146k (7), BBL 3k-71k (9). The catalog's "24h volume 6k" was taken on a day with no games. So the "thin, nobody watching" premise is false.

2) SPEED. I pulled goal wall-clock stamps from ESPN's public soccer summaries (keyEvents.wallclock) for 48 goals in 17 La Liga 2 and 2. Bundesliga games on 09-19 and 09-20. 46 of them matched to Kalshi markets. Kalshi's first print at least 8c away from the 4-minute pre-goal level came a median 7 s BEFORE ESPN's own goal stamp. 33 of 34 reactions came before the stamp; 12 goals had no move of 8c within 120 s either side. ESPN's publication delay comes on top of its stamp and was not measured.

3) WHERE THE STALE SUPPLY GOES. Across 294 price jumps in 41 games (all takers combined): 78k contracts were bought at stale prices in the first 10 s after the jump, 13k in 10-30 s, 5.5k in 30-60 s.

4) THE TEST THAT DECIDES IT (no future data used). Trigger: the first print at least 10c from the median of the prior 4 minutes. Entry: buy the side that moved up at the first print on that side, L seconds later. Score: 5-minute markout after the taker fee, clustered by game. Results (standard error in brackets): L=10 s: -0.61c (0.88); L=20: -0.47c (0.87); L=30: -1.25c (0.93); L=60: -0.87c (0.88); L=90: -0.56c (0.84). That is 200-228 moves in 34-38 games. A control that buys a random side at a random time scores -1.34c (0.64). So after 10 s there is nothing left beyond ordinary spread and fee. By league at L=30: La Liga 2 -0.9c, 2. Bundesliga -2.2c, KBO -4.0c, NPB +1.2c (2.5), 3. Liga -0.6c (2.3, 20 games), BBL +5.0c. The BBL figure is only 21 moves in 5 games, and one +52c move drives it; without that move it is +2.7c with an SE of about 3c. Kalshi has only 9 settled BBL games because the series began this month.

5) ARTEFACT CAUGHT. My first version picked jumps using the price 2-6 minutes later and showed +2.3c at L=30 (t about 4). That was look-ahead. The honest version above is -1.25c.

6) ENTRIES TIMED BY ESPN'S GOAL STAMP. Buying the scoring team D seconds after the stamp: D=0: +1.7c (0.9); D=5: +2.2c; D=10: +2.1c; D=20: +1.5c (0.9); D=30: +0.7c (0.8); D=60: +1.0c (0.7); D=90: -0.9c. That is 28-33 goals in 15 games. Profit at settlement is +5 to +8c, but its SE is 4-6c, so it is noise. This is the only positive cell, it is one of seven lags checked, and the larger causal sample contradicts it. Supply at that entry: contracts printed at or below the entry price within 30 s had a median of about 40 per goal (mean 115-190). That is everyone's supply, not ours.

Smallest effect the sample could detect: about 2.5c per contract.

chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
Expected: $0 a day at the $900 bank and $0 a day at $5k. Buying after the move, at any delay a free feed can reach (10 s or more after the market's first reaction), scored -0.5 to -1.25c per contract after fees. That is no better than random entries. A bigger bank does not help, because the limit is supply, not capital.

Most optimistic ceiling. This assumes the unproven ESPN-timed cell is real, AND that ESPN publishes within 20 s of its own stamp (not measured), AND that we take every contract every taker took:
- About 16 goals a day across La Liga 2, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga: 81 games in 14 days = 5.8 games a day, times 2.8 goals per game in the ESPN sample.
- Per goal: about 120 contracts at +2c = about $2.40.
- Total: 16 x $2.40 = about $38 a day.
At 30 s after the stamp the same arithmetic gives 190 x 0.7c = about $1.30 per goal, or about $21 a day. That cell's 95% range includes zero (-0.9c to +2.3c).
We would realistically get a fraction of that supply, and the fills we did get would be the adversely chosen ones: goals still under VAR review, or slow market makers.
chk.worst_case:
Proposed size of 100 contracts per goal at about 65c: roughly $65 at risk per position.
- A goal later cancelled by VAR (the video review) reverses the 20-40c move within seconds: -$20 to -$40 per position. Those are exactly the goals whose price was still stale when a slow feed saw them.
- If the game result flips, the full stake is lost: -$65.
- A busy Saturday with about 16 positions where 10 lose: about -$210.
chk.killer_risks:
1) Speed. The market moves a median 7 s before ESPN even timestamps the goal, and most stale offers are gone within 10 s. Any free feed (ESPN, openligadb, thesportsdb) publishes after that. What is left costs spread plus fee: -0.5 to -1.25c per contract, the same as random entries.
2) Adverse selection. A stale price still sitting there 30 s or more after a goal is disproportionately a goal under VAR review or a disputed event. That is the population a slow bot would fill.
3) Small samples where anything looked positive. BBL has 9 games ever, and its +5c comes from one +52c move. The ESPN-timed cell is 32 goals in 15 games at t about 2, one of 7 lags checked.
4) Scores are correlated within a game. 294 jumps are only 41 independent games; all standard errors above are clustered by game.
chk.next_test:
Only if we want to close the one open cell. It costs nothing and is read-only: a paper watcher for 2 weekends (about 60-80 goals).
- During La Liga 2, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga games, poll ESPN's summary endpoint (site.web.api.espn.com/apis/site/v2/sports/soccer/{esp.2|ger.2|ger.3}/summary?event=ID) every 2 s.
- Log when each goal first APPEARS against its wallclock stamp.
- At that moment, snapshot the Kalshi orderbook of the scoring team's market (GET /markets/{t}/orderbook), and again 5 minutes later.
Pass bar, to be written down before reading: over at least 60 goals, the average 5-minute markout of buying at the best ask when the goal appears is +2c or more after fee, with the lower 95% bound above 0 (clustered by game), AND the median size at or below that ask is at least 50 contracts.
Anything less and the idea stays dead. Expect it to fail: the stamp alone is already 7 s after the market has moved.
chk.capital_needed: None meaningful. Supply is the limit, not the bank: about 40 contracts per goal is the median printed at the entry price, or about $25 of stake. The $900 bank covers it.

Scratch folder: C:/Users/Joe/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--kals-repo/47b37ac1-655c-4d72-a81b-a48e9625d5bd/scratchpad/sweep/check-I59/

WHAT KILLS IT: Kalshi's pregame sports prices already sit on top of the sharpest bookmaker's line. Once you pay the taker fee and cross the bid-ask gap, there has been no 3c gap to buy, either now or in the past week.

1) LIVE COMPARISON. Scripts: snap.py and poll.py; output in snap_2026*.json and poll.out; analysis in leadlag.py. For the sharp line I used Pinnacle's no-vig moneyline, read from the free JSON feed its own public website uses (guest.api.arcadia.pinnacle.com); it answered from this machine. I compared it with the Kalshi books, every 60 s for 22 snapshots between 15:03Z and 15:24Z on 2026-09-25. Coverage was about 212 Kalshi team markets (~100 games): 16 MLB, 15 NFL, 46 NCAAF, 14 MLS and 9 ATP/WTA. I hand-checked the matching (right teams, home/away, MLS draw leg). "Fair" is the no-vig price; for each side I used whichever of two no-vig methods was less favourable to us. That gives 9,332 market-side-snapshots:
- After fee and the ask price, 77 were positive. Every one was under 1c (best +0.82c).
- Gaps of 2c or more: 0. Gaps of 3c or more: 0. Median -2.1c.
- Kalshi mid minus Pinnacle fair: median -0.04c; median absolute gap 0.64c; 99th percentile 2.90c; max 3.08c. That is the mid, before paying half the spread and the fee.
- Pinnacle's line moved 1c or more 10 times in the 22 minutes. Kalshi followed within about 2 minutes twice and did not move in the other 8. None of those moves opened a gap of 2c or more after fee.
- NHL (Pinnacle lists no preseason games) and WNBA (no open Kalshi games) could not be tested.

2) HISTORY: THE 'NEWS LAG' CASE. Scripts tape.py, tape_mlb2.py, tape_nfl.py, tape_ncaaf.py; rows in tape_rows*.json. The question: in Kalshi's own pregame trade history, did any buyer get a price that Kalshi itself moved 3c or more past, after fee, within 10, 30 or 60 minutes? That is what a stale-price pickoff after a pitcher scratch or injury would leave behind. Kick-off for football is taken as occurrence_datetime minus 3h; checked against the data, 5-minute price swings jump from about 1c to 9c exactly at that time.
- MLB, 90 clean games (09-18 to 09-24), 12h before each game: 16.2M contracts traded.
- NFL week 3 plus Thursday, 16 games, 6h before kick-off (covers the inactives window): 15.4M contracts.
- NCAAF 09-19, the 24 biggest games, 6h before kick-off: 6.2M contracts.
- Total: 37.8M contracts across 130 games.
- Pregame price range per game: MLB median 3c / max 7c; NFL median 2c / max 3c; NCAAF median 1c / max 5c.
- Buyers who ended up 3c or more ahead after fee: zero at 10 min and zero at 30 min. At 60 min: 9 MLB trades worth $21, against $26 on the mirror side, so noise.
- Buyers' average result after fee at +10 min: MLB -0.72c to -0.97c per contract, NFL -1.46c, NCAAF -0.96c. That means takers pay, and no informed pickoff pool exists.
- Upper bound: 0 events in 130 games puts the true rate below about 2.3% of games (95% confidence).

ARTEFACTS FOUND AND REMOVED (these are the ways a good number here would be fake):
(a) My first pass matched Kalshi's games for 09-26 and 09-27 to Pinnacle's lines for 09-25 (same teams, different day and pitchers). It printed 10 fake gaps of 3c or more, up to +10.7c. Fixed by matching MLB on the start time encoded in the ticker.
(b) KXMLBGAME-26SEP191910DETCWS was actually played in the afternoon (in-play from about 18:00Z), while its ticker says 19:10 ET. It produced a fake $15k 'pregame pool'. Excluded; everything else was $0.

Collectors alive after all jobs (pids 105352 and 2532788); 84.4 GB free disk.
chk.realistic_dollars_per_day:
$900 bank: about $0 a day in trading gains, because nothing qualified: 0 of 9,332 live market-side-snapshots and 0 of 37.8M past pregame contracts. The data costs money: The Odds API at $30-100 a month is -$1 to -$3.30 a day, so the net is -$1 to -$3.30 a day (or $0 using Pinnacle's free web feed, which carries a terms-of-service risk). $5k bank: the same, about $0 gross and -$1 to -$3.30 a day net. The bank size does not matter because there is no signal to size up.

Generous ceiling: take the 95% upper bound of fewer than 2.3% of games having a news gap, at about 30 in-season games a day. That is at most about 0.7 events a day. At 3c on about 200 contracts, each event is worth about $6, so under $4 a day. That assumes we beat Kalshi's professional market makers, who are clearly already pricing off the same sharp line (Kalshi mid within 0.64c of Pinnacle).
chk.worst_case: The strategy's main risk is a bot that believes a fake gap. My own first pass matched tomorrow's Kalshi game to today's line and showed ten 3-to-10c 'edges' that were really fair-priced bets on a different pitcher matchup. A bot with that bug would repeatedly buy what are actually coin-flips at fair prices. It would lose about 1.5-2.5c per contract on average (fee plus crossing the bid-ask gap) and could lose the full stake of each position. At 200 contracts near 50c that is about -$100 a game, and a whole slate of bad matches could lose several hundred dollars in one day. A second fake source is a rescheduled game whose ticker time is wrong: in-play prices get read as pregame gaps. Otherwise the worst case is simply the $30-100 a month data bill for nothing.
chk.killer_risks:
- Kalshi's pregame sports books are already priced off the sharp line. Mid is within 0.64c of Pinnacle's no-vig price (99th percentile 2.9c), and the taker fee plus half the spread is about 1.4-2.3c. So the gap before fee is below what it costs to take.
- The news-lag version needs a line jump of about 5c or more while Kalshi stays stale. None happened in 130 games and 37.8M contracts, including MLB lineup windows and the NFL inactives window. Where Kalshi did lag Pinnacle by about 2 minutes, the moves were 1.3-3.6c, inside the fee band.
- Anyone who can capture a real jump is racing professional market makers with direct feeds. A 60-second API poll (The Odds API caches) would arrive last. The fills we would get are the adversely selected ones: someone chose to sell to us.
- Pinnacle's free feed is the website's own internal API; using it in a bot may breach Pinnacle's terms. The paid alternative has a real monthly cost with no offsetting income.
- Matching bugs (wrong date or doubleheader, rescheduled start time) create fake large edges. Both kinds appeared in this check.
chk.next_test: None is worth paying for. If the operator wants the news case closed completely at zero cost: run snap.py/poll.py unchanged every 60 s through one NFL Sunday (15:30-17:30Z, the inactives window) and a week of MLB lineup windows (0-4h before first pitch). Pass bar, written before looking: at least 5 distinct games in the week where Kalshi's ask sits at or below Pinnacle no-vig minus fee minus 3c, for at least 2 consecutive snapshots, with at least 100 contracts at that price. Fewer than 5: stays dead. Cost: about 10 Kalshi reads a minute during those windows only, no orders, no subscription.
chk.capital_needed: None worth committing. Pregame positions would tie up capital from hours to about 2 days before settlement (NFL/NCAAF markets list days ahead), but there is no signal to deploy it on.
